database-systems-map.outcome: Take one real (or realistic) data-modeling decision you face and draw its Database Systems Map: the storage engines in play, the directed write/read/index/replication flow between them, the suspect edge where integrity or freshness can break, and the system class you choose to model in — then start the artifact that carries the rest of this course.
database-systems-map.proof: Section 1 of schema_migration_decision_and_rollback_packet.md: a directed map of the relevant storage systems (OLTP store, replica, index/cache, analytics sink), the suspect edge marked, the system class chosen with the constraint that forced it, and an explicit out-of-scope boundary. A reviewer traces a single write from commit to query-visible without you narrating.
database-systems-map.unlock: Your map shows directed flow across at least three real storage systems, marks the suspect edge, names the system class you chose and why, and draws a defended scope boundary.
database-systems-map.doNotClaim: Do not claim you have a systems map if you only named 'a database'. 'We use Postgres' is a product, not a map. The skill is showing where the truth lives, where copies of it lag, and which edge can serve a stale or inconsistent answer under load.

database-systems-map.text: A design review: the team wants to add a leaderboard query, someone says 'just put it in the database,' and the staff engineer asks one question - 'which database, and is it allowed to be five minutes stale?' The room stalls, because nobody mapped where the data actually lives versus where it gets read.

Every data model lives inside a system of stores - a source-of-truth OLTP engine, its replicas, an index or cache, an analytics sink - each with different consistency, isolation, and freshness guarantees. The Systems Map is the smallest accurate picture of those stores and the flow between them, and it is Section 1 of the migration-and-rollback packet you carry through this whole course.

database-systems-map.prompt: 'Let's just store it in Postgres.' Before you agree - what has that sentence already silently decided about your data? Answer before reading on.
database-systems-map.reveal: It pre-decided three things you have not earned: that you need ACID transactions (not just eventual consistency), that a single relational engine can serve both your writes AND your read patterns, and that the truth and the read copy are the same place. The real frame is a system class question: 'writes need a transactional source of truth with strong constraints, BUT the leaderboard read is high-fan-out and tolerates 60s staleness - so the truth lives in an OLTP store and the read is served from a derived index that lags.' Naming the product first feels decisive while quietly choosing the consistency model for you.

database-systems-map.title: Directed flow across stores + suspect edge + chosen system class - kept small on purpose
database-systems-map.text: Name the storage systems the decision touches, the direction data flows (write, replicate, index, analyze), the edge where freshness or integrity can break, and the system class you chose (OLTP relational, document, key-value, columnar, search) with the constraint that forced it. As small as it can be while still holding the failure.

database-systems-map.subtitle: Five stores on the write -> replicate -> index -> analyze path. Postgres is the source of truth; the suspect edge (Primary -> CDC -> Search Index) is where the catalog goes stale. The data warehouse and cache are deliberately scoped to show, but only the suspect edge is in play.

database-systems-map.title: Writing Section 1, one line at a time
database-systems-map.subtitle: The same map as text in schema_migration_decision_and_rollback_packet.md - built up store by store, with the system-class decision made explicit.
database-systems-map.code:
## 1. Database Systems Map
[App] --write (txn)--> [Postgres Primary]  (source of truth: ACID, constraints, isolation)
                            |--streams WAL--> [Read Replica]   (async, lags ~seconds)
                            |--CDC index----> [Search Index]   (derived, eventually consistent)
                            |--nightly ETL--> [Warehouse]      (columnar, analytics only)
[App] --catalog query------------------------> [Search Index]  (reads here, NOT the primary)
- System class chosen: OLTP relational for the truth (needs constraints + multi-row transactions)
- Forced by constraint: order writes must be atomic and referentially valid; cannot lose a paid order
- Suspect edge: Primary -> CDC -> Search Index (freshness gap; a new product is query-invisible until indexed)
- Blast radius if it fails: search shows a stale catalog; conversions drop; NO data loss (truth intact in primary)
- Boundary we will NOT cross: the analytics warehouse path is out of scope for this decision

steps.label: The source of truth
steps.note: Pick the engine that holds truth and the guarantees it owes you: ACID transactions, constraints, isolation. This is the one store a write is not 'done' until it commits to.

steps.label: The derived copies
steps.note: Replica and Search Index are COPIES, not truth. Mark them async - this is where lag and stale reads hide. A read served here can be seconds-to-minutes behind the primary.

steps.label: The analytics sink
steps.note: Columnar warehouse, batch-loaded. Different system class (column store, not row store) because the query pattern is aggregate scans, not point lookups.

steps.label: The read path
steps.note: The App queries the Search Index, NOT the primary. Whoever forgets this ships a feature that reads stale data and calls it a bug later.

steps.label: System class + the constraint that forced it
steps.note: State the class (OLTP relational) and the non-negotiable that ruled out alternatives: atomic, referentially-valid order writes rule out a plain key-value store as the truth.

steps.label: Suspect edge + blast radius
steps.note: The freshness gap lives on Primary -> CDC -> Search. Name that stale-catalog is recoverable (truth is intact) - stale is not lost, and that distinction sets urgency.

steps.label: The boundary
steps.note: Warehouse is out of scope - and you can defend why: nothing on the user-facing read path touches it.

database-systems-map.caption: A peer should trace one new product from its committed INSERT to 'appears in search' along these arrows - and point to exactly where it can be invisible for minutes.

database-systems-map.title: Two maps of the same data model
database-systems-map.subtitle: Both are true. Only one lets the team choose the storage system on purpose.

left.label: One-box 'the database'
lines: Single box labeled 'Database'
No distinction between truth and derived copies
No flow direction (write vs read vs index)
Consistency + isolation model never stated
Stale-read failures look like mystery bugs
left.verdict: Picks a product, hides the system class decision

right.label: Systems map
lines: Source of truth separated from derived copies
Directed write -> replicate -> index -> analyze
Suspect (lagging) edge marked explicitly
System class named + the constraint that forced it
Blast radius distinguishes stale (recoverable) vs lost
right.verdict: Chooses the engine for the guarantees it owes

database-systems-map.caption: Smaller and directed beats 'one big database'. The map's job is to surface where truth lives and where copies lag - the two facts every later schema, index, and migration decision depends on.

database-systems-map.text: The senior tell is naming guarantees, not products. 'Postgres' tells a reviewer nothing; 'a transactional source of truth with foreign-key constraints and read-committed isolation, fronted by an eventually-consistent search index' tells them exactly what can break and where. A sound design principle is choosing the data model and consistency guarantees BEFORE the implementation - the map is how you make that choice visible and reviewable.

database-systems-map.question: What most distinguishes a useful Database Systems Map from naming your database product?
options: It uses an official diagramming tool instead of a whiteboard sketch.
It lists every microservice and table in the company so nothing is omitted.
It separates the source of truth from derived copies, shows directed flow, marks where freshness or integrity can break, and names the system class chosen with the constraint that forced it.
It records which team owns each database for the on-call rotation.
database-systems-map.explanation: Usefulness comes from showing guarantees and flow: which store holds truth (with its ACID/constraint/isolation guarantees), which stores are lagging copies, where a stale or inconsistent read can be served, and why the chosen system class fits the constraint. Completeness (2) reintroduces the clutter that hides the suspect edge; the tool (1) and ownership (4) are not the modeling decision.

database-systems-map.intro: Prove your Systems Map earns its place - no hand-waving:
items: Every connection has a direction and a kind (write / replicate / index / analyze). An undirected line cannot tell a write path from a read path - fix it.
Exactly one store is marked as the source of truth, and you can state the guarantees it owes: transactions, constraints, and isolation level.
Every other store is labeled as a derived copy with its freshness behavior (synchronous, async-lagging, or batch).
The suspect edge - where a read can be served stale or where integrity can break under load - is marked and findable in under five seconds.
The blast radius distinguishes stale-but-recoverable from lost, and you can defend at least one store you left out as off the path.

prompts: Trace one write through your map out loud - from the transaction that commits it to the moment a user can query it - naming every async hop where it could lag.
Explain the system class you chose and the single constraint that ruled out the alternatives, using your own map as the example.
Defend the source-of-truth boundary: why is your truth store the one place a write is not 'done' until it commits, and what would break if a derived copy were treated as truth?

database-systems-map.text: This is cartography of where truth lives and where it lags - and it travels to any data-bearing system. A payments platform maps the ledger (strong, transactional) apart from the reporting replica (eventually consistent) before anyone designs a schema. An IoT pipeline maps the time-series store apart from the rollup table the dashboard reads. What stays invariant: separate the source of truth from its derived copies, show directed flow, mark the lagging edge, and choose the system class for the guarantees it owes. What changes with scale, latency, and privacy: how many copies, how stale they may be, and which constraints are non-negotiable. You have mapped the system; the next lessons keep this exact packet and add the schema, the constraints, and the migration-with-rollback that must preserve truth across this map under change, load, and bad input.

entities-relationships.outcome: Take one real domain (orders, patients, courses — your pick) and model it as entities + relationships: name each entity and its primary key, draw the relationships with explicit cardinality, and enforce every relationship with a foreign-key constraint. Then package the change as schema_migration_decision_and_rollback_packet.md.
entities-relationships.proof: schema_migration_decision_and_rollback_packet.md containing: the entities + PKs, the relationships with cardinality, the FK constraints (DDL), the rejected denormalized option, the expected failure (an orphaned row), the verification method, and the rollback script. A reviewer can trace one row from child to parent and back without you narrating.
entities-relationships.unlock: Every relationship in your model is enforced by a foreign-key constraint with a named cardinality — no relationship lives only in your head or in application code.
entities-relationships.doNotClaim: Do not claim you 'modeled the relationship' if the link exists only as a matching column name (orders.user_id with no FK). A column that happens to hold an id is not a relationship — the database does not know it is one, and it will let orphans in. The constraint IS the relationship.

entities-relationships.text: An order in production points at customer_id 8842. That customer was deleted last quarter. No FK was ever declared, so the database happily kept the orphan — and now the monthly revenue report sums orders whose customer no longer exists, and finance is asking why the numbers do not reconcile.

An entity is a thing you store rows about; a relationship is how two entities connect, and cardinality says how many. This is Section 1 of the schema_migration_decision_and_rollback_packet.md you carry through the rest of this course — schema, constraints, indexes, and migrations all stand on the entities and relationships you name here.

entities-relationships.prompt: An orders table has a customer_id column whose values match ids in the customers table. Is that a relationship the database will protect? Decide before reading on.
entities-relationships.reveal: No. Matching values are a convention, not a constraint. Until you declare FOREIGN KEY (customer_id) REFERENCES customers(id), the database treats customer_id as a plain integer — it will accept an order for a customer that never existed and let you delete a customer that still has orders. The relationship only becomes real, and only stays true under bad input, when a foreign-key constraint enforces it. The invariant of relational modeling: every reference points at a row that exists.

entities-relationships.title: A relationship is a foreign key with a cardinality, not a matching column
entities-relationships.text: An entity has a primary key. A relationship is a foreign key on the child pointing at the parent's primary key, with a stated cardinality (one-to-many, many-to-many). The invariant: no foreign key may reference a row that does not exist — that is referential integrity, and the constraint enforces it.

entities-relationships.subtitle: Four entities on the order path. Each relationship is a FK with a cardinality; the join table resolves the many-to-many; the suspect edge is the un-enforced reference that lets orphans in.

child with an enforced foreign key

entities-relationships.title: The schema for the model, one constraint at a time
entities-relationships.subtitle: DDL from the migration packet — entities become tables, relationships become foreign keys, cardinality becomes column rules.

steps.label: The parent entity + its primary key
steps.note: customers is an entity: one row per real customer. The PRIMARY KEY id is what every relationship will point at — pick a stable surrogate key, not email, which can change.

steps.label: The one-to-many relationship
steps.note: customer_id REFERENCES customers(id) IS the relationship. NOT NULL makes it mandatory (every order has a customer); the FK makes it real (every customer_id points at a row that exists).

steps.label: Cardinality via ON DELETE behavior
steps.note: ON DELETE RESTRICT blocks deleting a customer who still has orders — the database refuses the orphan at the source. This is the rule the mission's broken system never had.

steps.label: The many-to-many, resolved by a join entity
steps.note: An order has many products and a product is on many orders. You cannot store that with one FK — order_items is the join entity, two FKs plus a composite PK so the same product cannot be added to an order twice.

steps.label: CASCADE vs RESTRICT is a modeling decision
steps.note: ON DELETE CASCADE on order_id: deleting an order removes its items (they cannot exist without it). RESTRICT on product_id: you must not delete a product still on live orders. Same syntax, opposite intent — chosen per relationship.

steps.label: Index the foreign key
steps.note: A FK is not auto-indexed in Postgres. Without idx_orders_customer, 'all orders for this customer' scans the whole table and the query plan degrades as orders grow.

entities-relationships.caption: Run the proof: INSERT an order with customer_id = 99999 (no such customer). The FK rejects it. That rejection is the whole skill working.

entities-relationships.title: Two models of the same domain
entities-relationships.subtitle: Both store orders and customers. Only one preserves truth when a customer is deleted or a bad id arrives.

left.label: Convention-only model
lines: orders.customer_id is a plain BIGINT — no FK
Relationship lives in app code ("we always join on it")
Many-to-many flattened: product names stuffed in a TEXT column
Delete a customer → orders silently orphaned
Bad id 99999 inserts fine; report breaks weeks later
left.verdict: Integrity is a hope, not a guarantee

right.label: Enforced ER model
lines: customer_id REFERENCES customers(id), NOT NULL
Relationship lives in the schema — DB enforces it
Many-to-many resolved by order_items join entity
ON DELETE RESTRICT blocks the orphan at the source
Bad id 99999 is rejected at INSERT, not discovered in a report
right.verdict: Referential integrity holds under bad input

entities-relationships.caption: The convention model is faster to type and fails silently. The enforced model fails loudly at write time — which is the only time a failure is cheap to fix.

entities-relationships.text: The senior tell: they decide ON DELETE behavior per relationship before writing the FK, because it encodes meaning. CASCADE says 'this child cannot exist without its parent' (order items); RESTRICT says 'this parent is referenced, refuse to orphan it' (a product on live orders); SET NULL says 'the link is optional, keep the row.' Grounded in the relational integrity rules of the SQL standard, the constraint is where the domain rule lives — not in a code comment.

entities-relationships.question: You need to model that an order contains many products and a product appears on many orders. What is the correct relational structure?
options: Add a products TEXT column on orders and store a comma-separated list of product ids.
Add an order_id column on products so each product points back to its order.
Create a join entity (e.g. order_items) with a foreign key to orders and a foreign key to products, and a composite primary key.
Add a product_id column on orders; if an order has several products, insert duplicate order rows.
entities-relationships.explanation: A many-to-many relationship cannot be expressed by a single foreign key on either side — that only models one-to-many. You resolve it with a join entity carrying one FK to each parent and a composite PK that prevents duplicate pairings. Option 1 destroys referential integrity (you cannot FK a comma-list); option 2 forces a product into exactly one order; option 4 duplicates the order entity and corrupts its identity.

entities-relationships.intro: Prove your model holds — DDL diff and a dry run, not vibes:
items: Every entity has a primary key. If a table has no PK, it is a bag of rows, not an entity — a row you cannot uniquely name cannot be referenced.
Every relationship is a declared FOREIGN KEY, not just a matching column name. Grep your DDL: each *_id should appear in a REFERENCES clause.
Run the orphan test: INSERT a child row with a non-existent parent id. It MUST be rejected. If it succeeds, the relationship is not enforced.
Run the integrity test: try to DELETE a parent that still has children. RESTRICT must block it (or CASCADE must remove the children) — confirm the behavior matches what you intended.
Every many-to-many is resolved by a join entity with a composite PK — no comma-lists, no duplicated parent rows.
Each FK has an index. Check the query plan for 'orders for one customer' uses the index, not a sequential scan.

prompts: Explain, using your own model, why a matching column name is not a relationship but a FOREIGN KEY constraint is. What can the database do once the constraint exists that it could not before?
Walk a junior through one of your ON DELETE choices: which relationship is it on, did you pick CASCADE or RESTRICT, and what domain rule does that choice encode?
Why does a many-to-many relationship force a third entity, when one-to-many needs only a single column? Use your join table as the example.

entities-relationships.text: The same move runs in any domain: patients and visits (one-to-many, FK on visit), students and courses (many-to-many, resolved by an enrollment entity), authors and books. What stays invariant is referential integrity — every foreign key points at a row that exists. What changes is cardinality and the ON DELETE rule, because the domain's meaning of 'this child cannot exist without its parent' changes. You have named the entities and enforced the relationships; the next lesson takes this exact schema and adds the constraints and indexes that keep it correct and fast as the data grows — and your schema_migration_decision_and_rollback_packet.md carries forward as the capstone's first artifact.

normalization-denormalization.outcome: Take one schema that must change (or a realistic one) and write the decision packet: state whether you normalize to 3NF or deliberately denormalize a read path, name the integrity constraint you refuse to lose, the rejected option, and the rollback that restores truth if the migration goes wrong.
normalization-denormalization.proof: schema_migration_decision_and_rollback_packet.md: the selected normal form (or the named denormalization + its sync mechanism), the constraint that protects the invariant, the rejected approach, a DDL diff, and a rollback script. A reviewer reads it and can name what breaks if a duplicated field drifts.
normalization-denormalization.unlock: Your packet names the normal form, the constraint that guards the invariant, the rejected option, and a rollback that restores a single source of truth.
normalization-denormalization.doNotClaim: Do not claim you 'denormalized for performance' if you never measured the query plan it was meant to fix and never wrote the mechanism that keeps the duplicated data in sync. A copied column with no sync rule is not an optimization — it is an update anomaly waiting for production.

normalization-denormalization.text: A customer's old address ships their refund to a house they moved out of two years ago — because the orders table stored a copy of the address that was never updated when they changed it. One duplicated column, one update anomaly, one very real package at the wrong door.

Normalization decides where each fact lives once; denormalization decides where you knowingly duplicate it to make a read fast. Get the boundary wrong and the database stops telling the truth under change — which is the one job the schema you carry through this course must never fail.

normalization-denormalization.prompt: An orders table stores customer_email in every row so reports don't need a join. A customer changes their email. What just happened to your data? Answer before reading on.
normalization-denormalization.reveal: You now have two versions of one fact and no rule saying which is true. That is an update anomaly: the email lives in two places, the UPDATE touched one, and every old order row still carries the stale value. The relationship 'a customer HAS an email' was supposed to live on the customer entity exactly once. Copying it felt faster until the day the copies disagreed — and a database whose copies disagree cannot answer 'what is this customer's email?' at all.

normalization-denormalization.title: Normalize so each fact lives once; denormalize only with a sync rule
normalization-denormalization.text: Normalization removes redundancy: every fact lives in exactly one place, enforced by keys and constraints, so an update can't create two truths. The invariant: one fact, one home. Denormalization breaks that on purpose for read speed — and is only legitimate when you attach the mechanism that keeps the copy in sync.

normalization-denormalization.title: Where update anomalies are born — and repaired
normalization-denormalization.subtitle: Top path: the duplicated-column failure. An email lives in both customers and orders; an UPDATE hits one, and a read sees two truths. Bottom path: normalize the email onto its one entity, join to read — anomaly gone.

nodes.label: Update anomaly
nodes.description: one row updated, old orders stale

legend.label: the failure path: duplication -> drift -> two truths
the join that recombines normalized facts
the repair: one fact, one home

normalization-denormalization.title: The DDL diff inside the decision packet
normalization-denormalization.subtitle: Normalize the duplicated email to 3NF, enforce the invariant with a foreign-key constraint, and keep a rollback that restores the source of truth.

steps.label: The redundant column
steps.note: customer_email copied into every order is the transitive dependency 3NF forbids: email depends on customer, not on order.

steps.label: One transaction
steps.note: Wrap the migration so a failure mid-flight rolls back atomically — isolation means readers never see a half-applied schema.

steps.label: The foreign key IS the invariant
steps.note: The FK constraint makes 'every order points at a real customer' a database law, not a hope. This is the integrity you refuse to lose.

steps.label: Backfill before you drop
steps.note: Reconcile any row where the canonical value is missing BEFORE deleting the copy. Drop first and you destroy the only truth for orphan rows.

steps.label: Drop the duplicate
steps.note: The redundant fact is gone; the email now lives in exactly one place. The anomaly is structurally impossible now.

steps.label: Rollback restores from truth
steps.note: If the migration must reverse, re-add the column and refill it from customers.email — the source of truth — never from a backup of the stale copies.

normalization-denormalization.caption: The rollback rebuilds the duplicated column from the single source of truth, not from the data that was wrong in the first place.

normalization-denormalization.title: Denormalize blindly vs. denormalize with a contract
normalization-denormalization.subtitle: Same goal: make the dashboard's per-customer order-count query fast. Only one stays true under change.

left.label: Copied column, no sync rule
lines: Added customers.order_count, set once at write time
No trigger, no job, no constraint keeping it current
A refund deletes an order; the counter never decrements
Now two facts disagree: COUNT(*) vs the cached number
No query plan was ever measured to justify it
left.verdict: An update anomaly sold as an optimization

right.label: Measured + a sync mechanism
lines: Proved the join was slow with EXPLAIN on real volume
Denormalized order_count WITH a trigger on insert/delete
The trigger is the contract that keeps the copy true
Reconciliation job re-derives it nightly as a backstop
Documented: chosen, rejected (no-cache), reversal condition
right.verdict: A defensible trade: speed bought, truth kept

normalization-denormalization.caption: Denormalization is legitimate only when the duplicate carries a mechanism that keeps it in sync with its source — and you measured the query plan that made it worth the risk.

normalization-denormalization.text: The senior tell is not 'normalize everything' — it is 'normalize by default, denormalize on evidence.' The relational model starts from one-fact-one-home; a pro deviates only with a measured query plan AND a named sync rule, and writes both into the migration. 'It felt slow' is not evidence, and a copy with no sync rule is not a cache — it is a future incident.

normalization-denormalization.question: A reviewer asks for the exact evidence that your denormalization is safe, not just fast. Which response actually proves it?
options: "The dashboard feels snappier now, and the team is happy with it."

"Here is the EXPLAIN showing the join was the bottleneck, the trigger that keeps the duplicated count in sync on insert and delete, a reconciliation job as backstop, and the rollback that drops the column and re-derives from the source of truth."
"We denormalized because joins are always slow at scale."
"We added the column and a comment in the code telling people to keep it updated."
normalization-denormalization.explanation: Only option 2 shows the full contract: a measured query plan justifying the duplication, an enforced sync mechanism (trigger) so the copy cannot silently drift, a reconciliation backstop, and a rollback that restores from the single source of truth. The others are vibes ('feels snappier'), a myth ('joins are always slow'), or a hope ('a comment telling people to update it') — none of which survive a refund deleting a row.

normalization-denormalization.intro: Prove your packet keeps truth under change — no vibes:
items: Point to the one place each fact lives. If any non-key field is duplicated across tables, name the sync mechanism that keeps the copies equal — or normalize it away.
Run the DDL diff against a copy of prod (a migration dry run). It must apply cleanly and the foreign-key constraint must hold on existing rows.
Compare the query plan before and after (EXPLAIN). A denormalization with no measured plan improvement has no justification — revert it.
Execute the rollback script on the migrated copy: it must restore the schema AND refill any dropped column from the source of truth, not from stale data.
Run the constraint test: attempt an insert that violates the invariant (an order with a non-existent customer_id) and confirm the database rejects it.

prompts: In your own words: what is an update anomaly, and why does it make a database unable to answer a question it used to answer?
Explain the difference between 'normalize for correctness' and 'denormalize for performance' using your own schema — and name the constraint that protects the invariant in each case.
Walk through your rollback: why must it refill a restored column from the source of truth rather than from a backup of the duplicated values?

normalization-denormalization.text: This is the move anywhere one fact gets copied for speed: a denormalized analytics warehouse keeps a star schema fast but pairs every duplicated dimension with an ETL job that reconciles it; a cache layer is denormalization with a TTL and an invalidation rule as its sync mechanism; even a spreadsheet that copies a price into a hundred rows is an update anomaly waiting to happen. What stays invariant: one fact has one home, and every deliberate copy carries a contract that keeps it true. What changes is the mechanism — trigger, ETL job, cache invalidation — chosen by how much staleness the user, the latency budget, and the cost can tolerate. Carry the schema_migration_decision_and_rollback_packet.md into the database capstone: it is the same packet — schema, migration, query-plan, constraint, and rollback proof — that proves you can make a model change without making the data lie.

constraints-invariants.outcome: Take one real entity in your schema (orders, accounts, bookings) and write its invariants as DATABASE constraints — NOT NULL, UNIQUE, CHECK, FK, and an EXCLUDE — then capture the decision and the rollback in schema_migration_decision_and_rollback_packet.md so the truth survives bad input, concurrency, and a failed migration.
constraints-invariants.proof: schema_migration_decision_and_rollback_packet.md: each business invariant mapped to a concrete constraint (with the DDL), the rejected app-layer-only option, an expected-failure autopsy, a verification method (constraint test + migration dry-run + rollback script), a reviewer objection, and the capstone connection. A peer can read the packet and reproduce the migration AND the rollback from it.
constraints-invariants.unlock: Every named invariant is enforced by a constraint in the database (not just app code), and the packet contains a working forward migration plus a tested rollback.
constraints-invariants.doNotClaim: Do not claim an invariant is 'enforced' if the only thing enforcing it is application code or a code review habit. App validation is advisory; the database constraint is the guarantee. An invariant a second writer can violate under concurrency was never enforced.

constraints-invariants.text: Two services write to orders at the same millisecond; both pass the app's "is this email taken?" check, both insert, and now one customer has two accounts that billing will fight over for a year. The app validated. The database did not — so the truth quietly broke.

A constraint is an invariant the database itself refuses to violate — true after every INSERT, UPDATE, and concurrent transaction, with no cooperation from application code. This is Section: Constraints of the migration packet you carry into the database capstone.

constraints-invariants.prompt: Your app checks `if not email_exists(email): insert(user)` before every signup, and code review is strict. Is the "one account per email" rule safe? Decide before reading on.
constraints-invariants.reveal: No — it has a race. Two requests run `email_exists` at the same instant, both see "free," both insert. The check-then-act gap is invisible in single-threaded testing and fatal under load. The database does not have the gap: a UNIQUE constraint makes the second INSERT fail atomically, because the engine enforces it inside the same isolation boundary as the write. App code guards a door; a constraint welds it shut.

constraints-invariants.title: An invariant becomes real only when the database enforces it
constraints-invariants.text: Name the rule that must always hold (unique email, non-negative balance, no double-booked room). Express it as a constraint — UNIQUE, CHECK, FK, NOT NULL, EXCLUDE — so the engine rejects any write that breaks it, even under concurrency. App checks advise; constraints guarantee.

constraints-invariants.title: Where a violated invariant is caught — app guard vs database constraint

constraints-invariants.title: Writing the constraints, one invariant at a time
constraints-invariants.subtitle: The forward migration in the packet — every business rule mapped to a constraint the engine enforces.

steps.label: INV-1 — NOT NULL + UNIQUE
steps.note: This is the race from the pretest, closed for good. UNIQUE is enforced by an index inside the write's isolation boundary, so the second concurrent INSERT fails with 23505 instead of duplicating the row.

steps.label: INV-2 — CHECK keeps money honest
steps.note: balance >= 0 is a per-row invariant. A withdrawal that would overdraw is rejected by the engine, not by a hopeful `if amount <= balance` in three different services.

steps.label: INV-3 — FK = referential integrity
steps.note: An order can't point at a deleted account. ON DELETE RESTRICT makes the database refuse to orphan rows; the relationship between the two entities is now a guarantee, not a convention.

steps.label: INV-4 — EXCLUDE for overlap
steps.note: The invariant app code can't express: 'no two bookings for the same room overlap in time.' An EXCLUDE constraint over a range type enforces it across all writers — the kind of rule a UNIQUE can't reach.

steps.label: One transaction, all-or-nothing
steps.note: Wrapping in BEGIN/COMMIT means the migration is atomic: if INV-4 fails to build, INV-1..3 roll back too. You never land in a half-enforced schema.

constraints-invariants.caption: On a hot table, ADD CONSTRAINT takes a lock and validates every existing row — the gold path adds it NOT VALID first, then VALIDATE CONSTRAINT in a second step to avoid blocking writes. The compare block shows why.

constraints-invariants.title: Enforce the invariant in app code vs in the schema
constraints-invariants.subtitle: Same rule — 'balance never goes negative.' One is a hope; one is a guarantee.

Re-implemented in transfers, refunds, admin tools
Two concurrent withdrawals both read balance=100
Both pass the check, both debit → balance=-50
A backfill script bypasses the service entirely
Invariant is true only where someone remembered it

Enforced for every writer, every code path, forever

Backfill, psql, ORM, cron — all bound by it
Migration adds it NOT VALID then VALIDATE (no long lock)
Rollback script drops it to restore prior schema

constraints-invariants.caption: Push the invariant down to the lowest layer that can enforce it. App validation gives fast, friendly errors; the constraint is the floor that catches everything app validation missed.

constraints-invariants.text: The senior tell: a constraint that's never been rolled back hasn't been proven. Before you ship ADD CONSTRAINT on a live table, write and run the DROP CONSTRAINT rollback in a dry-run first — and on a hot table add it `NOT VALID`, then `VALIDATE CONSTRAINT` separately, so validation doesn't hold an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock while production waits. A hard-won maintenance lesson: an invariant you can't safely reverse is a liability, not a guarantee.

constraints-invariants.question: A reviewer says: "You added a UNIQUE constraint on `email` in one migration that runs ALTER TABLE ... ADD CONSTRAINT on a 40-million-row production table during peak traffic." What is the strongest objection?
options: UNIQUE constraints are slower than application-level checks, so this hurts read performance.
Building the unique index to validate 40M rows takes a long lock that blocks writes; split it — CREATE UNIQUE INDEX CONCURRENTLY, then attach it — and ship a tested rollback.
UNIQUE can't enforce one-account-per-email; only application code can do that correctly.
You should use a CHECK constraint instead of UNIQUE for email.
constraints-invariants.explanation: The invariant choice (UNIQUE) is right — option 3 inverts reality, since the constraint is exactly what closes the race app code can't. The real production failure is operational: validating 40M rows under a blocking lock stalls writes. The gold path builds the index CONCURRENTLY off the critical path, attaches it, and carries a tested rollback. Option 1 misframes correctness as a read-perf tradeoff; option 4 picks a constraint type that can't express uniqueness.

constraints-invariants.intro: Prove your invariants are enforced — no vibes:
items: For each business rule, point to the exact constraint (UNIQUE / CHECK / FK / NOT NULL / EXCLUDE) that enforces it. If the only enforcement is app code, it is not enforced — fix it.
Run the constraint test: attempt the violating write directly in psql (bypass the app) and confirm the database rejects it with the right error (e.g. 23505, 23514, 23503).
Run the migration as a dry-run inside a transaction you ROLLBACK — confirm it applies cleanly against a copy of real data, not an empty table.
Open your rollback script and actually run it after the forward migration; confirm the schema returns to the last-known-true state with no orphaned objects.
On any hot table, confirm the constraint is added NOT VALID then VALIDATE (or index built CONCURRENTLY) so validation never holds a blocking lock.
Confirm the packet records one expected-failure autopsy: what breaks, which writer, and which constraint catches it.

prompts: In your own words: why is an invariant enforced only by application code not actually enforced? Use your own UNIQUE-vs-app-check example.
Walk a junior through one constraint in your migration and the exact rejected write that proves it works — name the error code the engine returns.
Explain why you add a constraint NOT VALID then VALIDATE separately on a large table, in terms of locks and what production sees during the migration.

constraints-invariants.text: The same move governs any system where truth must survive bad input and concurrency. A ledger enforces double-entry as a CHECK that debits equal credits, not a nightly reconciliation hope. A scheduler enforces 'no overlapping shifts' as an EXCLUDE, not a busy app loop. The invariant that stays invariant is the one pushed to the layer that can't be bypassed. You've now written Section: Constraints of schema_migration_decision_and_rollback_packet.md — the same packet the database capstone reuses, where you'll pair these constraints with the migration, query-plan, data-quality, and backup proof. Carry it forward: not "I understand constraints" but "here is the migration that made an invariant unbreakable, and the rollback that proves I can take it back."

indexes-access-patterns.outcome: Take one real read path your app runs hot (a filtered, sorted, paginated query) and design the index that serves it from the ACCESS PATTERN backwards — then prove the planner uses it. Capture the call in schema_migration_decision_and_rollback_packet.md: the query, the chosen index, the rejected index, the EXPLAIN before/after, and a rollback.
indexes-access-patterns.proof: Section 'Indexes & Access Patterns' of schema_migration_decision_and_rollback_packet.md: the exact query (filter + sort + limit), one CREATE INDEX whose column order matches the access pattern, an EXPLAIN (ANALYZE) showing an Index Scan replacing a Seq Scan, the rejected index with why, and a DROP INDEX rollback. A reviewer runs your EXPLAIN and sees the plan change.
indexes-access-patterns.unlock: Your index column order is derived from the query's equality → sort → range columns, and EXPLAIN proves the planner chose it over a sequential scan.
indexes-access-patterns.doNotClaim: Do not claim a query is 'indexed' because a column appears somewhere in an index. If the planner still shows Seq Scan or Sort, the index does not serve that access pattern — a column that exists in an index but in the wrong position is invisible to the query.

indexes-access-patterns.text: The orders page that loaded in 40ms for 10,000 rows now takes 9 seconds at 4 million — same query, same code, untouched. Someone added an index last quarter; the planner ignores it, because it was built for a column order no real query asks for.

An index is not decoration on a table; it is a data structure shaped for a specific access pattern. Pick the pattern wrong and you pay a write tax for a structure no read uses — this is Section 'Indexes & Access Patterns' of the migration packet you carry through the module.

indexes-access-patterns.prompt: Your query is WHERE tenant_id = ? AND status = ? ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20. You add INDEX(created_at, tenant_id, status). It's still slow. Why — the columns are all there?
indexes-access-patterns.reveal: A B-tree is sorted left-to-right, so the FIRST column decides everything. Leading with created_at means the index is ordered by date across all tenants — to satisfy tenant_id = ? the planner must scan the whole tree. The rule is equality columns first, then the sort column, then ranges: INDEX(tenant_id, status, created_at). Now the equality predicates jump to a contiguous slice already ordered by created_at, so the LIMIT 20 reads 20 rows and stops — no sort, no scan.

indexes-access-patterns.title: The access pattern designs the index — equality, then sort, then range
indexes-access-patterns.text: Read the query, not the table. Order composite-index columns: equality filters first (they pin a slice), then the ORDER BY column (so the slice arrives pre-sorted), then range filters. The invariant: the index's left prefix must match how the query narrows and sorts, or the planner can't use it.

indexes-access-patterns.title: How the planner chooses: query → index match → scan path
indexes-access-patterns.subtitle: The same query meets two indexes. A left-prefix match yields an Index Scan that stops at LIMIT; a mismatched leading column forces a Seq Scan + Sort. The decision node is the failure path AND the repair path on one map.

indexes-access-patterns.title: Designing the index from the query, then proving it
indexes-access-patterns.subtitle: The real artifact: query → composite index in equality/sort/range order → EXPLAIN diff → rollback. Each line is a forcing function in the migration packet.
indexes-access-patterns.code:
-- ## Indexes & Access Patterns
-- Hot access pattern (the read we are serving):
SELECT id, total FROM orders
 WHERE tenant_id = $1 AND status = 'open'
 ORDER BY created_at DESC
 LIMIT 20;

-- Chosen index: equality (tenant_id, status) -> sort (created_at)
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_orders_tenant_status_created
  ON orders (tenant_id, status, created_at DESC);

-- Rejected: leading with the sort column
-- CREATE INDEX idx_orders_created_tenant ON orders (created_at, tenant_id);
--   why rejected: created_at first => filter can't pin a slice => Seq Scan

-- Proof (run before and after the CREATE):
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT id, total FROM orders
 WHERE tenant_id = $1 AND status = 'open'
 ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20;

-- Rollback:
DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_orders_tenant_status_created;

steps.label: Read the access pattern first
steps.note: Equality columns: tenant_id, status. Sort column: created_at DESC. Bound: LIMIT 20. The index is designed FROM these four lines, never from the table definition.

steps.label: Column order = equality, then sort
steps.note: (tenant_id, status, created_at DESC): the two equality predicates pin a contiguous slice, and created_at DESC means that slice is already in the order the query wants — the LIMIT reads 20 and stops.

steps.label: CONCURRENTLY = no write lock
steps.note: On a live 4M-row table, a plain CREATE INDEX takes an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock and blocks writes. CONCURRENTLY trades a slower build for zero downtime — a migration-safety call, not a performance one.

steps.label: Name the rejected option
steps.note: Leading with created_at is the seductive wrong answer: the column you sort by feels like it should come first. It can't pin the equality slice, so the planner falls back to Seq Scan + Sort. Writing down why you rejected it is the reviewable judgment.

steps.label: EXPLAIN is the proof, not the vibe
steps.note: Run it before and after. 'Seq Scan on orders ... rows=4000000' must become 'Index Scan using idx_orders_tenant_status_created ... rows=20' with the Sort node gone. No plan change = no proof.

steps.label: Rollback ships with the change
steps.note: DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY is the reversal condition. An index migration without a written rollback is a one-way door pretending to be reversible.

indexes-access-patterns.caption: A reviewer pastes your EXPLAIN into psql and watches Seq Scan (rows=4000000) collapse to Index Scan (rows=20). That diff is the deliverable.

indexes-access-patterns.subtitle: Query: WHERE tenant_id=? AND status='open' ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20. Both contain all three columns. Only one serves the access pattern.

Leading column is the SORT, not a filter

EXPLAIN: Seq Scan + Sort, rows=4,000,000
Write tax paid for a read nobody gets
left.verdict: Indexed on paper, Seq Scan in production

right.label: Access-pattern index
lines: idx(tenant_id, status, created_at DESC)
Equality columns first → slice is pinned
Sort column last → slice arrives pre-sorted
EXPLAIN: Index Scan, rows=20, no Sort node
LIMIT 20 reads 20 leaf entries and stops

indexes-access-patterns.caption: Equality before sort before range. A column in the wrong position is invisible to the query — completeness of columns is not correctness of order.

indexes-access-patterns.text: The senior tell is reading EXPLAIN, not trusting CREATE INDEX. Every index is a standing write cost: each INSERT (and each UPDATE touching an indexed column) has to update every matching index, not just the table. So a pro deletes the indexes no query plan actually uses as fast as they add the one the hot path needs — an unused index is pure tax with no service.

indexes-access-patterns.question: For WHERE org_id = ? AND archived = false ORDER BY updated_at DESC, which composite index lets the planner skip the sort and avoid a full scan?
options: INDEX(updated_at, org_id, archived) — put the sort column first so results come out ordered.
INDEX(org_id, archived, updated_at) — equality columns first, then the ORDER BY column.
INDEX(org_id), INDEX(archived), INDEX(updated_at) — three single-column indexes so each predicate is covered.
INDEX(archived, org_id, updated_at) — the most selective-sounding column first.
indexes-access-patterns.explanation: Equality predicates (org_id, archived) must lead so the B-tree pins one contiguous slice; updated_at last means that slice is already ordered, so the planner reads it in reverse and skips the Sort. Leading with updated_at (1) can't pin the slice → Seq Scan. Three separate indexes (3) force a slower bitmap combine and still need a sort. Reordering equality columns (4) doesn't help the sort — and 'most selective first' is a single-column heuristic, not a composite-ordering rule.

indexes-access-patterns.intro: Prove the index serves the access pattern — no vibes:
items: Run EXPLAIN (ANALYZE) before and after CREATE INDEX. 'Seq Scan' must become 'Index Scan using <your index>', and the standalone 'Sort' node must disappear.
Confirm column order is equality → sort → range. If a range or sort column sits before an equality column, the prefix is broken — reorder it.
Check the planner actually picked it: the index name appears in the plan. An index that exists but is absent from EXPLAIN is serving no one.
Confirm the index is reachable by writes safely: CREATE/DROP use CONCURRENTLY on a live table, and the packet names the lock trade-off.
Write the rollback (DROP INDEX) and the rejected index with its reason. A migration with no reversal and no rejected option is not reviewable.

prompts: Explain to a teammate why 'all the columns are in the index' does not mean the query is served — use the left-prefix rule and your own EXPLAIN.
Walk through how you ordered your index columns: which were equality, which was the sort, and why the sort column had to come after the equality ones.
Name one index you would DROP as a result of this lesson, and the write cost it was charging for a plan no query uses.

indexes-access-patterns.text: The move is universal: design the structure backwards from how it is read, then prove the read uses it. A MongoDB compound index follows the exact same Equality-Sort-Range rule; a DynamoDB table forces you to name the partition key (equality) and sort key up front before you write a single row; even a search engine's field ordering obeys it. What stays invariant is 'the access pattern designs the index, and EXPLAIN is the proof'; what changes is the engine's vocabulary and its write-cost ceiling. Carry this packet into the database capstone — the same schema_migration_decision_and_rollback_packet.md must show the query, the access-pattern index, the EXPLAIN diff, and the rollback, reused unchanged in structure.

query-design-joins.outcome: Take one real query that joins an entity to a one-to-many child (orders → line_items, customers → payments) and design the JOIN so its grain is correct: write the query, prove the result count and any SUM is right, then capture the decision in schema_migration_decision_and_rollback_packet.md.
query-design-joins.proof: A section of schema_migration_decision_and_rollback_packet.md showing: the join grain you intended (one row per WHAT), the query, a query-plan note (which join strategy + which index), and a row-count + aggregate check proving the join did not fan out and double-count. A reviewer can re-run the check and get the same number.
query-design-joins.unlock: Your query states its intended grain, returns exactly that grain, and you have a count/SUM check that fails on the naive fan-out version and passes on yours.
query-design-joins.doNotClaim: Do not claim the join is correct because it 'ran' and returned rows. A fan-out join runs fine and returns a plausible-looking SUM that is silently 3x too high. 'It returned data' is not proof of grain — a row-count or aggregate check against a known truth is.

query-design-joins.text: The finance dashboard shows $4.2M in revenue. The ledger shows $1.4M. Nobody touched the numbers — someone added a JOIN to orders → line_items and the SUM(order_total) quietly tripled, once per line item. The query ran green the whole time.

A JOIN is not 'glue between tables' — it changes the grain of your result set, the unit each row represents. Get the grain wrong and every COUNT, SUM, and AVG downstream is wrong while the query still succeeds. This is Section 2 of the migration packet you carry through the module.

query-design-joins.prompt: You join orders (1 row each) to line_items (3 rows each) and SELECT SUM(orders.total). One order, total = $100, has 3 line items. What does the SUM return — and why is that the trap? Answer before reading.
query-design-joins.reveal: It returns $300. The JOIN fans the single order row out to three rows (one per line item), so orders.total is repeated three times and summed three times. The query is valid SQL, the plan is optimal, the result is wrong by exactly the child cardinality. The grain silently shifted from 'one row per order' to 'one row per line item' — and your aggregate followed it.

query-design-joins.title: A JOIN sets the grain; aggregate at the grain you mean
query-design-joins.text: Every join multiplies rows by the matched cardinality. A one-to-many join makes the parent's grain become the child's. The invariant: SUM/COUNT the parent only at the parent's grain — aggregate the child first, then join, or your totals inherit the fan-out.

query-design-joins.title: Where the fan-out happens — and the repair path
query-design-joins.subtitle: orders (grain: one row per order) joined to line_items (one row per item) fans 1 order → 3 rows. SUM(order_total) over that grain triple-counts. The repair: pre-aggregate line_items to order grain, THEN join.

legend.label: fan-out failure — grain shifted to the child
repair — pre-aggregate child to parent grain
correct grain, correct total

query-design-joins.title: The query, stepped — fan-out vs. pre-aggregated join
query-design-joins.subtitle: Same question ('total revenue per customer, with item counts'), two grains. Only the second keeps SUM honest.
query-design-joins.code:
-- ✗ NAIVE: joins straight to line_items → fan-out
SELECT c.id, c.name,
       SUM(o.order_total)      AS revenue,   -- triple-counted
       COUNT(li.id)            AS item_count
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o      ON o.customer_id = c.id
JOIN line_items li ON li.order_id  = o.id   -- grain becomes 1 row / item
GROUP BY c.id, c.name;

-- ✓ REPAIR: pre-aggregate line_items to ORDER grain, then join
WITH item_rollup AS (
  SELECT order_id,
         COUNT(*) AS item_count
  FROM line_items
  GROUP BY order_id                          -- 1 row / order, no fan-out
)
SELECT c.id, c.name,
       SUM(o.order_total)        AS revenue,  -- counted once
       SUM(ir.item_count)        AS item_count
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o      ON o.customer_id = c.id
JOIN item_rollup ir ON ir.order_id = o.id    -- grain stays 1 row / order
GROUP BY c.id, c.name;

-- PROOF: revenue must equal the independent ledger total
SELECT SUM(order_total) AS truth FROM orders;  -- compare to query output

steps.label: The grain claim
steps.note: This query intends 'one row per customer'. SUM(o.order_total) is only correct if each order row appears once — but the next line breaks that.

steps.label: The fan-out edge
steps.note: Joining line_items multiplies each order by its item count. The result grain is now 'one row per line item', and order_total is duplicated across them.

steps.label: Pre-aggregate the child
steps.note: The CTE collapses line_items to one row per order BEFORE the join. This is the move: fix the grain at the source, not after.

steps.label: Join at parent grain
steps.note: Now orders ⋈ item_rollup is 1:1 on order_id. order_total appears exactly once per order, so SUM is honest.

steps.label: The proof query
steps.note: An independent SUM(order_total) over orders alone is ground truth. If the joined revenue equals this, the grain held. If it is a multiple, you fanned out.

query-design-joins.caption: Index note: ensure line_items(order_id) and orders(customer_id) are indexed — the planner picks a hash/merge join on them; without the index it falls to a nested loop that scans line_items per order.

Join is 1:1 on order_id — grain stays per-order
SUM(order_total) counted exactly once

query-design-joins.caption: The tell is never 'did it run' — it is 'does the join's grain match the grain your aggregate assumes'. Pre-aggregate the many-side first.

query-design-joins.text: Senior reviewers read a JOIN by asking one question first: 'what is one row here?' If you cannot state the grain in a sentence, the SUM cannot be trusted. CS2023's Data Management knowledge area covers relational query design and data integrity; SWEBOK V4 has no query-design or database content. A fan-out join violates row-level integrity invisibly, which is exactly why it caps a lesson without a proof: the result is plausible, never verified.

query-design-joins.question: Your report joins invoices to a one-to-many payments table and SUM(invoice_amount) looks too high. What is the correct fix?
options: Add SELECT DISTINCT to remove duplicate rows before the SUM.
Pre-aggregate payments to the invoice grain (GROUP BY invoice_id) in a subquery/CTE, then join so each invoice row appears once.
Switch the INNER JOIN to a LEFT JOIN so no rows are dropped.
Add an index on payments.invoice_id so the SUM runs faster.
query-design-joins.explanation: The SUM is inflated because the one-to-many join fanned each invoice out across its payments, duplicating invoice_amount. Pre-aggregating payments to invoice grain restores a 1:1 join so invoice_amount is summed once. DISTINCT (1) collapses identical rows but silently drops legitimately-equal amounts and breaks COUNT; LEFT JOIN (3) changes which rows appear, not the fan-out; an index (4) makes the wrong number arrive faster.

query-design-joins.intro: Prove the join's grain — no vibes:
items: State, in one sentence, what one row of your result represents ('one row per customer'). If you cannot, you have not designed the grain yet.
Run COUNT(*) of your result vs. COUNT(DISTINCT parent_id). If they differ, the parent fanned out — your aggregate is suspect.
Compare your SUM to an independent ground-truth aggregate over the parent table alone (SELECT SUM(order_total) FROM orders). Equal = grain held; a multiple = fan-out.
Read the query plan (EXPLAIN): confirm the many-side join uses an index on the FK (order_id), not a sequential scan inside a nested loop.
Confirm the proof query is pinned in schema_migration_decision_and_rollback_packet.md so a reviewer can re-run it and the rollback (drop the new join/view) restores the old report.

prompts: Explain 'grain' to a teammate using your own query: what does one row represent before the join, and what does it represent after?
Why does a fan-out join inflate SUM but leave the query valid and fast? What does that tell you about trusting 'it ran'?
Describe your repair: where exactly did you pre-aggregate the many-side, and how does the proof query confirm it worked?

query-design-joins.text: Same skill, any one-to-many: a CRM joining accounts → contacts inflates 'pipeline value' once per contact; an analytics query joining sessions → events triples 'revenue per session'; a billing migration joining subscriptions → invoices double-charges in a report. The invariant that stays: aggregate the many-side to the parent grain before joining, and prove totals against a parent-only ground truth. What changes is the integrity stake — a fan-out in a finance migration is a one-way door (you bill wrong), so the rollback script and query-plan check in schema_migration_decision_and_rollback_packet.md become mandatory, not optional. This packet is your capstone evidence: not 'I understand joins' but 'here is a join I designed, proved at grain, and could safely roll back.'

transactions-atomicity.outcome: Take one realistic multi-statement write (a money transfer, an order + inventory decrement, a multi-table migration) and make it ATOMIC: wrap it in one transaction so it either fully commits or fully rolls back, then capture the decision in schema_migration_decision_and_rollback_packet.md — context, the constraint you protect, the selected approach, the rejected approach, and the exact failure you fear.
transactions-atomicity.proof: schema_migration_decision_and_rollback_packet.md plus a transcript: run the multi-statement write, kill it mid-flight (raise an error between the two UPDATEs), and SELECT both rows afterward. A reviewer sees the database returned to its pre-transaction state — no half-applied write — and your packet names the invariant the transaction protected.
transactions-atomicity.unlock: Your write is wrapped in BEGIN/COMMIT with a ROLLBACK path, you demonstrated a mid-transaction failure leaving zero partial state, and your packet names the all-or-nothing invariant by which it was judged.
transactions-atomicity.doNotClaim: Do not claim atomicity because you wrote BEGIN. Atomicity is proven by the ABORT path, not the happy path. If you never showed a forced mid-transaction failure rolling everything back, you proved a successful insert, not an atomic unit of work.

transactions-atomicity.text: Account A is debited $500. Then — before the matching credit lands in Account B — the process is killed: a deploy, a deadlock, a network blip. The money has now simply evaporated, and the ledger that was supposed to hold the truth is the thing that lost it.

Real writes are rarely a single statement — a transfer is a debit AND a credit, an order is an insert AND an inventory decrement. Atomicity is the rule that fuses those statements into one indivisible unit: all of them commit, or none of them do, even when the process dies between them.

transactions-atomicity.prompt: You run two UPDATEs back-to-back with no transaction: debit A, then credit B. The first succeeds, then the connection drops before the second. What is the state of the database? Decide before reading on.
transactions-atomicity.reveal: Permanently half-applied: A is down $500, B is unchanged, and nothing will ever reconcile it — the debit already committed on its own. Without a transaction, each statement is its own atomic unit, so 'two statements' means 'two independent commits.' The fix is not more retries or careful ordering; it is declaring the two statements ONE unit with BEGIN/COMMIT, so the dropped connection rolls the debit back instead of leaving torn money in the ledger.

transactions-atomicity.title: Atomicity is all-or-nothing: the transaction is the indivisible unit
transactions-atomicity.text: A transaction groups statements so they commit together or abort together — there is no partial outcome. The invariant: at every point an observer can see, either all the writes happened or none did. A mid-flight failure must leave the database exactly as it was before BEGIN.

transactions-atomicity.title: The transfer as one atomic unit — commit path and abort path
transactions-atomicity.subtitle: BEGIN opens the unit; the debit and credit are staged inside it. A failure between them routes to ROLLBACK, restoring pre-transaction state. Only a clean COMMIT makes either write durable. The torn middle state is never observable.

COMMIT — every write becomes durable together

steps.label: The weak version
steps.note: No BEGIN means each UPDATE is its own atomic unit and commits independently. A failure after line 2 leaves the debit applied and the credit lost — torn money.

steps.label: BEGIN / COMMIT fuse the statements
steps.note: Everything between BEGIN and COMMIT is one unit of work. Until COMMIT runs, the writes are staged and reversible — not yet durable.

steps.label: Defend the invariant inside the unit
steps.note: A CHECK (balance >= 0) constraint evaluated mid-transaction aborts the whole transaction, not just the offending row — so a bad input can never leave a half-transfer.

steps.label: Force the abort — this is the proof
steps.note: SELECT 1/0 stands in for a real mid-flight failure. Postgres marks the transaction aborted; COMMIT can no longer succeed.

steps.label: Inspect the result
steps.note: Both rows are unchanged. The debit was rolled back with the credit it was never paired to. All-or-nothing resolved to NOTHING — exactly the guarantee.

transactions-atomicity.caption: Run the proof block: A is NOT down $500 afterward. The happy path shows insertion; the abort path is what actually demonstrates atomicity.

transactions-atomicity.text: Atomicity is the A in ACID: a transaction is the unit of recovery. (SWEBOK V4 has no 'data-management body of knowledge'; ACID/transaction concepts live in the ACM/IEEE CS2023 Data Management knowledge area, not SWEBOK.) The reviewer's lens is integrity under failure, not under success. Pair it with a CHECK constraint and you get two layers — the constraint refuses bad data, the transaction guarantees that refusal undoes the whole unit rather than half of it.

transactions-atomicity.question: A reviewer asks: 'Show me the exact evidence that this transfer is atomic and not just a happy-path answer.' Which response actually proves it?
options: Point to the BEGIN and COMMIT keywords in the code and explain that they group the statements.
Run the transfer once, SELECT both balances, and show the money moved correctly.
Force a failure between the debit and the credit, then SELECT both rows and show neither was changed — the whole unit rolled back.
Show that the accounts table has a CHECK (balance >= 0) constraint.
transactions-atomicity.explanation: Atomicity is the all-or-nothing guarantee under failure, so the only evidence that proves it is the abort path: a forced mid-transaction failure leaving ZERO partial state. Keywords (0) describe intent, the happy-path run (1) only shows a successful write, and the constraint (3) guards the value but does not by itself prove the debit rolls back with the failed credit.

transactions-atomicity.intro: Prove your write is atomic — under failure, not just under success:
items: Run the transaction once normally and confirm both writes landed (COMMIT path works).
Inject a failure BETWEEN the two writes (raise an error, divide by zero, kill the connection), then SELECT every affected row and confirm none changed — the abort path leaves zero partial state.
Confirm the constraint that guards the invariant (e.g. CHECK balance >= 0) aborts the whole transaction, not just the one statement, when violated mid-unit.
Confirm no statement that must be grouped is running outside the BEGIN/COMMIT — a stray UPDATE before BEGIN is its own commit and breaks the guarantee.
Confirm schema_migration_decision_and_rollback_packet.md names the invariant ('debit and credit commit together or not at all') and points to the abort transcript as proof.

transactions-atomicity.text: The same all-or-nothing move governs any multi-step change to shared truth. A schema migration that adds a column, backfills it, and adds a NOT NULL constraint must be one unit — a failure mid-backfill cannot leave a half-typed table, so the migration wraps its DDL + backfill in a transaction with a rollback script (the rejected option is the un-wrapped migration that strands the table). An order service decrements inventory AND inserts the order line atomically, or it oversells. What stays invariant: the database is never observable in a half-applied state. What changes is the unit's contents and the cost of the abort path — a money transfer rolls back in milliseconds; a 10-million-row backfill needs a batched, resumable strategy because one giant transaction would lock the table. Carry schema_migration_decision_and_rollback_packet.md into the database capstone: its DDL diff, migration dry run, rollback script, query-plan comparison, and constraint test are the exact proof the capstone reuses.

isolation-concurrency.outcome: Take one read-modify-write path in your schema (a counter, a balance, an inventory decrement) and write the isolation decision: name the concurrency anomaly it is exposed to, the isolation level or lock you will use to close it, the option you rejected, and the proof that it holds under two concurrent transactions.
isolation-concurrency.proof: Section of schema_migration_decision_and_rollback_packet.md covering isolation: the named anomaly (lost update / write skew / dirty read), the chosen guard (SERIALIZABLE or SELECT ... FOR UPDATE or a constraint), the rejected option, and a two-session transcript showing the anomaly under the weak level and its absence under the chosen one. A reviewer can replay both sessions and sees the same result.
isolation-concurrency.unlock: Your packet names the exact anomaly, the isolation level or lock that closes it, the rejected alternative, and a reproducible two-transaction proof — not a claim that 'transactions handle it'.
isolation-concurrency.doNotClaim: Do not claim a path is 'safe under concurrency' because you wrapped it in BEGIN/COMMIT. A transaction is atomic, not serializable — under READ COMMITTED two concurrent BEGIN/COMMIT blocks still lose updates. Atomicity is not isolation; naming the anomaly and the level that prevents it is the work.

isolation-concurrency.text: Two customers buy the last concert ticket within the same 40 milliseconds. Both transactions read inventory = 1, both subtract one, both COMMIT, and the table now reads inventory = 0 — but you sold two tickets to a single seat. No error fired. The lost update is invisible until the venue calls.

This lesson sits in the applied-skill phase of Databases and Data Modeling: you already model entities, constraints, and transactions, but a schema that is correct for one user can silently corrupt under concurrent ones. Isolation is the property that decides whether your invariants survive load — Section 4 of the migration-and-rollback packet you carry through this module.

isolation-concurrency.prompt: Two transactions both run BEGIN; UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 100 WHERE id = 7; COMMIT at the same time. Is the final balance guaranteed correct? Decide before reading on.
isolation-concurrency.reveal: Yes — and that is the trap that teaches the wrong lesson. balance = balance + 100 is a single atomic UPDATE, so the database locks the row and serializes the two writes for you. But the moment you split it into a READ then a WRITE — SELECT balance (app adds 100) UPDATE balance = 600 — both transactions read 500, both write 600, and one +100 vanishes. The anomaly is not in the transaction; it is in the read-modify-write gap, and only the isolation level decides what happens inside that gap.

isolation-concurrency.title: Isolation decides what concurrent transactions can see of each other's uncommitted gaps
isolation-concurrency.text: An isolation level is the contract for which anomalies — dirty read, lost update, write skew, phantom — are possible. The invariant: pick the weakest level (or narrowest lock) that still forbids the anomaly your schema's correctness depends on. Atomicity is free; serializability is not.

isolation-concurrency.title: The two-session proof inside the migration packet
isolation-concurrency.subtitle: The failure path (READ COMMITTED, oversells) and the repair (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE) — replayable in two psql sessions.
isolation-concurrency.code:
## 4. Isolation Decision
# Anomaly: lost update on inventory.qty (read-modify-write across app code)

# --- FAILURE: READ COMMITTED, two concurrent sessions ---
# Session A                          # Session B
BEGIN;                               BEGIN;
SELECT qty FROM inventory WHERE id=7;  -- A reads 1
                                    SELECT qty FROM inventory WHERE id=7;  -- B also reads 1
UPDATE inventory SET qty=0 WHERE id=7;
COMMIT;                             UPDATE inventory SET qty=0 WHERE id=7;  -- overwrites
                                    COMMIT;   -- qty=0, but TWO tickets sold

# --- REPAIR: take the row lock on read ---
BEGIN;
SELECT qty FROM inventory WHERE id=7 FOR UPDATE;  -- A locks the row
                                    -- B's SELECT ... FOR UPDATE now BLOCKS here
UPDATE inventory SET qty=qty-1 WHERE id=7 AND qty>0;
COMMIT;                             -- B unblocks, re-reads qty=0, sells nothing

# Rejected: SERIALIZABLE globally -> correct but serialization_failure
# retries under load; FOR UPDATE scopes the cost to this one hot row.

steps.label: Name the anomaly first
steps.note: Lost update on a read-modify-write — not 'concurrency bug'. The named anomaly is what the rest of the packet must close.

steps.label: Both sessions read the same value
steps.note: Under READ COMMITTED, B's SELECT sees the last committed value and does not block. Both read qty=1 — the gap is open.

steps.label: Second write silently wins
steps.note: A commits qty=0; B's UPDATE then overwrites with its own qty=0. No error — the database did exactly what each transaction asked.

steps.label: FOR UPDATE locks on read
steps.note: The repair: A's SELECT ... FOR UPDATE takes a row-level write lock, so B's identical SELECT blocks instead of reading stale data.

steps.label: Guarded decrement
steps.note: qty=qty-1 ... AND qty>0 is the real decrement. When B unblocks it re-reads qty=0, the WHERE fails, and zero rows change — the oversell is refused.

steps.label: Record the rejected option
steps.note: SERIALIZABLE is correct but converts the race into serialization_failure errors the app must retry. FOR UPDATE pays the cost only on the hot row — that tradeoff is the reviewable judgment.

isolation-concurrency.caption: Replay both blocks in two psql sessions: the first sells two tickets for one seat; the second blocks B until A commits, then refuses the oversell. That transcript IS the proof.

isolation-concurrency.text: Standards grounding (ACM/IEEE CS2023, Data Management): the SQL standard's four isolation levels are defined by which phenomena they forbid, and most databases do not match the names. (SWEBOK V4 does not cover SQL isolation levels; drop it as an authority here.) PostgreSQL's default is READ COMMITTED, its 'REPEATABLE READ' is actually snapshot isolation (which prevents lost updates but NOT write skew), and only SERIALIZABLE forbids write skew. Never reason from the level's name — reason from the anomaly it is documented to prevent on your engine.

isolation-concurrency.question: A reviewer asks: 'You set the transaction to REPEATABLE READ — does that make this transfer-between-accounts logic correct?' What is the right answer?
options: Yes — REPEATABLE READ is a high level, so all anomalies are prevented.

It prevents dirty reads and lost updates, but on Postgres's snapshot isolation it does NOT prevent write skew, so if the invariant spans two rows (e.g. 'both balances must stay >= 0') you still need SERIALIZABLE or an explicit lock.
No — only READ UNCOMMITTED is safe for transfers.
It does not matter, because BEGIN/COMMIT already makes it serializable.
isolation-concurrency.explanation: Write skew is the anomaly that survives snapshot isolation: two transactions each read a consistent snapshot, each check an invariant that holds, and each commit a change that — together — violate it. The classic case is two withdrawals that each see the combined balance as sufficient. REPEATABLE READ on Postgres is snapshot isolation and does not forbid it; SERIALIZABLE or SELECT ... FOR UPDATE on the read set does. Options 1 and 4 confuse atomicity with serializability.

isolation-concurrency.intro: Prove the isolation decision holds — no hand-waving:
items: Name the exact anomaly (dirty read, lost update, write skew, or phantom). 'Concurrency bug' is not a name and cannot be tested.
Run the two-session transcript: under the weak level the anomaly REPRODUCES, and under your chosen guard it does not. If you cannot reproduce the failure, you have not proven the fix prevents it.
Confirm the guard matches the anomaly: FOR UPDATE / SERIALIZABLE for write skew across rows; a UNIQUE or CHECK constraint where the invariant is single-row (let the engine reject, not the app).
Check the rejected option is recorded with its cost: global SERIALIZABLE buys correctness but adds serialization_failure retries — say why you did or did not pay it.

Confirm the rollback path is stated: the migration adds the lock/level change, and reverting it re-opens the anomaly — so the rollback note must flag that downgrade as a correctness regression, not a free revert.
