isolation-concurrency.text: The pattern is domain-independent: name the anomaly, pick the weakest guard that forbids it, prove it with a concurrent replay. A booking system fears double-booking (lost update); a ledger fears write skew across debit and credit rows; a job queue fears two workers claiming the same task (phantom on the unclaimed set, closed with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED). What stays invariant: correctness under concurrency is a property you must NAME and PROVE, never inherit from the default level. What changes: which anomaly the schema's truth depends on, and therefore how much isolation you are willing to pay for. This isolation section drops straight into the database capstone — the same migration-and-rollback packet, the same two-session proof, reused unchanged where the capstone schema has its own hot read-modify-write path.

migrations-schema-evolution.outcome: Take one real schema change you need to ship to a live, populated table (rename a column, add a NOT NULL, split a field) and write the schema_migration_decision_and_rollback_packet.md: the expand→backfill→contract plan, the forward DDL, the rollback DDL, and the constraint + query-plan proof that the change preserves truth without a downtime window.
migrations-schema-evolution.proof: schema_migration_decision_and_rollback_packet.md attached to the evidence ledger: context, selected expand-contract approach, the rejected single-shot ALTER, forward DDL diff, a runnable rollback script, the constraint test, and a before/after query-plan comparison. A reviewer can replay the migration on a copy and replay the rollback to the exact prior state.
migrations-schema-evolution.unlock: Your packet ships the change in reversible phases, proves the new constraint holds on existing rows, and includes a rollback that returns the schema to its prior state.
migrations-schema-evolution.doNotClaim: Do not claim a migration is safe because it ran on your empty local dev table. An empty table passes every constraint and locks nothing. The proof is that it preserves the existing rows and acquires no long-held lock on a populated table under writes.

migrations-schema-evolution.text: 2 a.m. deploy: a one-line ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN status TEXT NOT NULL takes a full table lock on 80 million rows, every checkout write blocks behind it, and the on-call watches the error rate go vertical for the eleven minutes it takes to rewrite the table. The column was trivial. The migration was the outage.

A schema is a contract that thousands of live rows and a running application already depend on; evolving it is changing the contract while both sides keep talking. This lesson turns 'I edited the schema' into a reviewable packet that preserves every existing row, locks nothing for long, and can be reversed — the artifact your database capstone reuses for every change.

migrations-schema-evolution.prompt: You need a new non-null column on a 50-million-row table. Two options: one ALTER that adds the column NOT NULL with a default in a single statement, or three smaller migrations. Which is safer — and why isn't the one-liner the obvious win? Decide before reading.
migrations-schema-evolution.reveal: The one-liner is a trap on older or strict engines: adding a NOT NULL column forces the database to verify or rewrite every existing row, taking a lock that blocks writes for the whole rewrite. The safe path is expand-contract: (1) add the column nullable (instant, metadata-only), (2) backfill in small batches with no global lock, (3) add the NOT NULL constraint as a separate, validatable step. Three migrations is slower to write and faster to ship safely — because none of them holds a long lock or strands a row.

migrations-schema-evolution.title: Evolve in expand → backfill → contract phases — never one destructive shot
migrations-schema-evolution.text: Add the new shape alongside the old (expand, reversible), move data in batches (backfill), then remove the old shape only after the app stops using it (contract). The invariant: at every phase the live app and existing rows stay valid, and each phase has a rollback.

migrations-schema-evolution.title: The packet's forward + rollback DDL, step by step
migrations-schema-evolution.subtitle: Renaming orders.email → orders.contact_email under live writes — expand, backfill, constrain, and the rollback that undoes it.
migrations-schema-evolution.code:
-- == FORWARD (expand-contract) ==
-- Phase 1 expand: instant, metadata-only, fully reversible
ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN contact_email text;          -- nullable on purpose

-- Phase 2 backfill: batched, no global lock, idempotent
UPDATE orders SET contact_email = email
  WHERE contact_email IS NULL AND id BETWEEN :lo AND :hi;  -- loop :lo/:hi over the table

-- Phase 3 constrain: validate the rule on already-populated data
ALTER TABLE orders
  ADD CONSTRAINT contact_email_present CHECK (contact_email IS NOT NULL) NOT VALID;
ALTER TABLE orders VALIDATE CONSTRAINT contact_email_present;   -- scans, does not block writes

-- Phase 4 contract: ONLY after the app reads/writes contact_email
ALTER TABLE orders DROP COLUMN email;

-- == ROLLBACK (reverse the latest phase only) ==
-- If we are pre-contract, the old column still exists — undo is cheap:
ALTER TABLE orders DROP CONSTRAINT IF EXISTS contact_email_present;
ALTER TABLE orders DROP COLUMN IF EXISTS contact_email;        -- back to the prior schema

steps.label: Expand is the safe move
steps.note: Adding a NULLABLE column is a metadata change — instant, no row rewrite, no long lock. This is why expand always comes first and is always reversible.

steps.label: Backfill in batches inside a transaction
steps.note: Bounding by id keeps each UPDATE small so it never takes a table-wide lock. WHERE contact_email IS NULL makes the migration idempotent — safe to re-run if it dies halfway.

steps.label: Add the constraint NOT VALID, then VALIDATE
steps.note: NOT VALID adds the rule instantly for new rows; VALIDATE scans existing rows separately without blocking writes. If a row is null, VALIDATE fails loudly — that is your constraint test, not a surprise outage.

steps.label: Contract last — and only after cutover
steps.note: Dropping email is the one irreversible step. It runs only once the app no longer reads the old column, so the expand phases can be rolled back freely until this line.

steps.label: The rollback IS part of the artifact
steps.note: Because contract hasn't run, the old column is intact: drop the new constraint and column and you are byte-for-byte back to the prior schema. A migration without this block is not reviewable.

migrations-schema-evolution.caption: A reviewer replays FORWARD on a copy of production data, then ROLLBACK, and confirms the schema returns to its exact prior state with every original row intact.

migrations-schema-evolution.text: The senior tell: a migration is reviewed by its rollback, not its forward. Anyone can write an ALTER. The engineer who writes the matching DOWN script — and can name the one phase (contract / drop) that crosses the point of no return — is the one whose migration gets merged. SWEBOK and ABET both frame this as the difference between a change and a controlled, verifiable change.

migrations-schema-evolution.question: A reviewer says: 'Show me the exact evidence this migration is not just a happy-path answer.' Which response points to real proof?
options: "It ran green on my local database with no errors."

"Here is the DDL diff, the rollback script that restores the prior schema, the VALIDATE CONSTRAINT run that passed on the existing rows, and the before/after EXPLAIN showing the new query uses the index instead of a seq scan."
"The new column has a sensible name and a comment."
"I added the NOT NULL in one ALTER so there are fewer steps to review."
migrations-schema-evolution.explanation: Only option 2 names inspectable artifacts that span the real risks: the DDL diff (what changed), a rollback (reversibility), a constraint validation against existing data (truth preserved), and a query-plan comparison (the change actually does what it was for). A green local run (1) proves nothing on a populated, concurrently-written table; fewer steps (4) is exactly the destructive shortcut.

migrations-schema-evolution.intro: Prove your migration packet holds — no vibes:
items: Run the forward DDL against a COPY of production-shape data (not an empty table). If it acquires a lock that blocks writes for more than a moment, your expand phase isn't metadata-only — split it.
Run the rollback script and diff the resulting schema against the original. If it isn't byte-for-byte the prior state, your DOWN is incomplete.
Run VALIDATE CONSTRAINT (or your constraint test) against the existing rows. A pass proves the rule holds on real data; a fail is the migration catching a violation before production does.
Capture EXPLAIN before and after. Confirm the new query path uses the intended index instead of a sequential scan — the change must be proven, not assumed.
Confirm the backfill is idempotent: kill it halfway, re-run it, and verify no row is double-written or skipped.

prompts: In your own words, why does adding a nullable column lock nothing while adding a NOT NULL column can rewrite the whole table? Use your own migration as the example.
Name the one phase in your packet that is irreversible, and explain why it must run last — after app cutover, not before.
Explain to a junior why VALIDATE CONSTRAINT on existing rows is the real proof, and why a green run on an empty dev table proves nothing.

migrations-schema-evolution.text: Expand-contract is not a Postgres trick — it is how you change any contract that two live parties depend on without taking the system down. A REST API deprecates a field by adding the new one, dual-writing, then removing the old (same three phases). A data pipeline evolves an event schema by tolerating both versions during the cutover. Anywhere existing data and a running consumer both depend on a shape, you expand, migrate, then contract — with a rollback for every phase. Carry schema_migration_decision_and_rollback_packet.md straight into the database capstone: it reuses this exact packet — DDL diff, rollback, constraint test, and query-plan comparison — as the proof that your capstone schema preserves truth under change, load, and bad input. Your portfolio claim is no longer 'I understand migrations'; it is 'here is a schema change I shipped to a populated table with zero downtime and a proven rollback — read it.'

query-plans-performance.outcome: Take one real (or realistic) slow query on a table you own, read its actual query plan with EXPLAIN ANALYZE, and write the decision packet: the plan before, the index or rewrite you chose, the rejected option, the plan after, and the rollback. The win is a measured plan change you can defend — not a hunch that an index will help.
query-plans-performance.proof: schema_migration_decision_and_rollback_packet.md with a before/after EXPLAIN ANALYZE diff (actual rows, actual time, the scan node that changed), the chosen index/rewrite, the rejected option with its reason, a rollback (DROP INDEX) script, and a constraint that stays true under the change. A reviewer reads the two plans and agrees the change is why it got faster.
query-plans-performance.unlock: Your packet shows a real query plan before and after, names the scan that changed (Seq Scan → Index Scan or a join reorder), and includes a rollback — no claim of speedup without the two plans.
query-plans-performance.doNotClaim: Do not claim a query is 'optimized' because you added an index and it 'feels faster'. Wall-clock from a warm cache is not proof — the buffer cache lies. The proof is the plan: the planner now chooses a cheaper node, with lower actual rows scanned, on a cold or representative run. An index the planner refuses to use is dead weight you still pay to maintain on every write.

query-plans-performance.text: The dashboard query that returned in 40ms on your laptop takes 9 seconds in production, and the on-call is staring at a table that grew from 10k rows to 40 million while you slept. Nobody guesses their way out of this — you ask the database one question: show me the plan.

A query plan is the database telling you exactly how it will fetch your data — which index, which scan, which join order, and how many rows it expects at each step. Read it before you touch a schema, because the wrong index is a write-time tax that buys you nothing, and the cheapest fix is often a rewrite, not a new structure.

query-plans-performance.prompt: Your query filters on `email`, there's an index on `email`, and it's still slow. Before you blame the database — why might the planner be ignoring your index? Answer before reading on.
query-plans-performance.reveal: Because for THIS query the index is the slow path, and the planner knows it. If the filter matches 30% of a 40M-row table, jumping to the index and back to the heap 12M times costs more random I/O than just reading the whole table sequentially — so a Seq Scan is correct. Indexes win on selectivity (few rows out of many). Wrap `email` in `LOWER(email)` or a leading-wildcard `LIKE '%x'` and the index becomes unusable entirely. The planner isn't broken; your mental model of 'index = fast' is. EXPLAIN shows you which world you're in.

query-plans-performance.title: Read the plan before you change the schema
query-plans-performance.text: EXPLAIN ANALYZE shows the planner's chosen scan, join order, and estimated-vs-actual rows. The invariant: a measured plan change is the proof of a speedup — never the index alone. If estimate and actual diverge wildly, the planner is flying blind; fix the stats, not the schema.

query-plans-performance.title: How the planner turns SQL into a plan — and where it goes wrong
query-plans-performance.subtitle: The same query takes the slow path (Seq Scan on a giant table) or the fast path (Index Scan). The decision hinges on selectivity and fresh statistics. The dashed edge is the failure: stale stats make the planner mis-estimate rows and pick the wrong scan.

nodes.label: Seq Scan
nodes.description: read all 40M rows — fast only if most rows match

nodes.label: Index Scan
nodes.description: jump via index — fast when few rows match

legend.label: the planner — picks a path by estimated cost
fast path: index used because few rows match
failure path: stale stats → wrong scan

query-plans-performance.title: Reading the real plan — before, fix, and after
query-plans-performance.subtitle: The worked expert example: a Seq Scan on 40M rows, the index that fixes it, and the EXPLAIN ANALYZE that proves the planner switched. This block is the heart of the packet.
query-plans-performance.code:
-- BEFORE: the slow query, with its actual plan
EXPLAIN ANALYZE
SELECT id, total FROM orders WHERE status = 'open' AND created_at > now() - interval '7 days';
--  Seq Scan on orders  (cost=0.00..921k rows=210000 width=20)
--                       (actual time=0.4..8932 ms  rows=180312  loops=1)
--    Filter: (status = 'open' AND created_at > ...)
--    Rows Removed by Filter: 39819688      <-- read 40M to keep 180k
--  Planning Time: 0.3 ms   Execution Time: 9021 ms

-- THE FIX: a partial composite index matching the WHERE shape
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_orders_open_recent
  ON orders (created_at)
  WHERE status = 'open';   -- partial: only index the rows we query

ANALYZE orders;            -- refresh stats so the planner trusts the index

-- AFTER: same query, re-planned
EXPLAIN ANALYZE
SELECT id, total FROM orders WHERE status = 'open' AND created_at > now() - interval '7 days';
--  Index Scan using idx_orders_open_recent on orders
--                       (actual time=0.05..41 ms  rows=180312  loops=1)
--  Execution Time: 47 ms       <-- 9021 ms -> 47 ms, plan node CHANGED

-- ROLLBACK (two-way door): the index is additive, drop reverses it
DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_orders_open_recent;

steps.label: Measure first, with ANALYZE
steps.note: EXPLAIN alone shows estimates; EXPLAIN ANALYZE actually runs it and reports actual rows + actual time. You cannot prove a speedup without the real numbers.

steps.label: Name the offending node
steps.note: Seq Scan on orders — the planner reads every row. The 'cost' is the planner's estimate; the 'actual time' is the truth. When they disagree, suspect stale statistics.

steps.label: The smoking gun
steps.note: Rows Removed by Filter: 39.8M. The query keeps 180k but the engine touched 40M to find them. That ratio — kept vs scanned — is the selectivity that decides whether an index helps.

steps.label: A partial composite index
steps.note: Index created_at, but WHERE status='open' so only open orders are indexed. Smaller index, cheaper writes, and it matches the exact query shape. CONCURRENTLY avoids locking the table in production.

steps.label: ANALYZE — or the index is invisible
steps.note: Fresh statistics let the planner trust the new index. Skip this and it may keep choosing the Seq Scan; the index then costs write time and earns nothing — the classic dead-weight failure.

steps.label: Prove the plan changed
steps.note: Index Scan using idx_orders_open_recent, 47 ms. The node TYPE changed — that is the proof, not the wall-clock alone. Same actual rows (180312), so the result is identical.

steps.label: Rollback = the reversal condition
steps.note: DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY reverses cleanly with no data loss. An index migration is a two-way door; this line is what lets you ship it without fear.

query-plans-performance.caption: The packet pastes both plans side by side. Same rows out (180312), one node type changed, 9021 ms → 47 ms. A reviewer reads it in ten seconds and agrees the index is why.

query-plans-performance.title: Two migration packets, same slow query
query-plans-performance.subtitle: Both add an index. Only one proves it did anything — and only one is safe to ship.

lines: Problem: 'orders query is slow'
Fix: CREATE INDEX on every column in the WHERE
Proof: 'ran it twice, second time was fast'
No EXPLAIN — never read the plan
Index on status (2 values) — planner ignores it
No ANALYZE, no rollback, locked the table to build it
left.verdict: Slower writes, unused index, second run was just warm cache

right.label: Measured decision packet

Chosen: partial index on created_at WHERE status='open'
Rejected: index on status alone (low selectivity, planner skips it)
After plan: Index Scan, 47ms — node type changed, same rows out
ANALYZE run, CONCURRENTLY build, DROP INDEX rollback attached

query-plans-performance.caption: Indexing the low-selectivity column (status, 2 distinct values) is the classic trap: the planner refuses it and you pay write cost forever. Selectivity, read from the plan, decides what to index.

query-plans-performance.text: The senior tell: read 'Rows Removed by Filter' and the estimate-vs-actual gap before you read anything else. If the planner expected 200 rows and got 200,000, your statistics are stale — run ANALYZE and re-plan before adding a single index. Half of 'we need an index' incidents are really 'we never ran ANALYZE after a bulk load,' and the planner was mis-estimating selectivity the whole time. Grounded in engineering discipline (and reinforced by SWEBOK V4's emphasis on evidence-based measurement): optimization decisions must be evidence-driven, and the query plan is the evidence. (SWEBOK V4 has no 'data-management knowledge area.')

query-plans-performance.question: A reviewer asks for proof your index actually sped up the query. Which is the convincing evidence?
options: The query ran in 50ms when you re-ran it after creating the index.
An EXPLAIN ANALYZE before (Seq Scan, 9s) and after (Index Scan, 47ms) showing the plan node changed and the same rows were returned.
The index exists — you can see it in \d orders.
Your ORM's query log shows a lower duration on the last request.
query-plans-performance.explanation: Only option 2 is proof. A faster re-run (1, 4) can be warm buffer cache, not the index — the planner might still be doing a Seq Scan over cached pages. The index merely existing (3) says nothing about whether the planner USES it. The before/after plans show the node type changed from Seq Scan to Index Scan with identical rows out — that, and only that, proves the index is the cause.

query-plans-performance.intro: Prove your plan change holds — no warm-cache illusions:
items: You captured EXPLAIN ANALYZE (not bare EXPLAIN) before AND after — actual rows and actual time, not just estimates.
The plan node visibly changed (Seq Scan → Index Scan, or a join reorder). If the node is identical, you have not proven the index did anything.
Actual rows returned match before and after — the change made it faster, not different. A speedup that changes results is a bug.
You ran ANALYZE after the index build and confirmed the planner actually chose the index — an index it ignores is dead weight that taxes every write.
A rollback (DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY, or the reverse migration) is in the packet, and you marked the change two-way-door — index migrations reverse with no data loss.
The constraint still holds under the change: a UNIQUE or NOT NULL the table guarantees is not weakened by the index or rewrite you chose.

prompts: In your own words: why is a faster wall-clock time on a re-run NOT proof that your index helped, and what is?
Explain selectivity using your own query: how many rows does the filter keep out of how many, and why does that number decide whether an index wins?
Walk through your before-plan: name the scan node, the 'Rows Removed by Filter', and the one line that told you the planner was reading the whole table.

query-plans-performance.text: The move travels to every query engine you'll meet. Postgres calls it EXPLAIN ANALYZE; MySQL has EXPLAIN ANALYZE and the FORMAT=TREE output; a data warehouse like BigQuery or Snowflake hands you a query profile with the same skeleton — scan, join order, rows in vs rows out, the spilled stage that's actually slow. What stays invariant: read the plan before you change the structure, prove the change by the node that moved, and never trust wall-clock over the plan. What changes is the cost model — a warehouse punishes a full-table shuffle, an OLTP store punishes random heap fetches — so the same plan can be right in one and wrong in the other. Your schema_migration_decision_and_rollback_packet.md is the first artifact of the database capstone: it already carries a before/after plan, a chosen-vs-rejected option, a constraint that survives the change, and a rollback. The capstone reuses it unchanged in structure — you don't talk about query performance now, you can prove it.

repository-data-access-layer.outcome: Take one real entity (say Order) and wrap its database access behind a repository: a single interface (findById, save, findByCustomer) that hides SQL, the schema, and the migration churn — then write the schema_migration_decision_and_rollback_packet.md that proves a column rename ships behind that interface without touching a single caller.
repository-data-access-layer.proof: schema_migration_decision_and_rollback_packet.md attached to the evidence ledger: context, the repository interface, the selected approach (expand/contract migration), the rejected approach (rename-in-place), expected failure, verification method (DDL diff + migration dry run + rollback script + query-plan compare + constraint test), reviewer objection, and capstone connection. A peer can rename orders.total_cents → amount_cents behind the repo and no caller changes.
repository-data-access-layer.unlock: Your repository is the ONLY path to the orders table, callers depend on the interface (not SQL), and your packet shows a schema change shipping + rolling back without a caller edit.
repository-data-access-layer.doNotClaim: Do not claim a repository if business logic still writes raw SQL anywhere else, or if your method signatures leak storage (returns a raw row, takes a WHERE-clause string). A leaky abstraction that callers must know the schema to use is a data-access layer in name only — the rename will still break them.

repository-data-access-layer.text: A 5-minute column rename — orders.total → total_cents — fans out into 47 broken call sites across three services, because every one of them wrote its own SELECT against the table. The team that wrapped that table in one repository renames the column, ships, and the diff touches a single file.

In the production-pressure phase, schemas change under load: columns rename, indexes get added, tables split. The repository is the seam that absorbs that change — it concentrates every query, constraint assumption, and transaction boundary for one entity in one swappable place, so migrations stay local.

repository-data-access-layer.prompt: Your service has SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = $1 written in 12 different files. A migration renames a column. How many files break — and what does that tell you about where the schema actually lives? Answer before reading on.
repository-data-access-layer.reveal: All 12 — because the schema doesn't live in the database, it lives smeared across every caller that hard-coded a query. The repository's whole job is to make the answer 'one'. When data access is centralized, the table's shape is a private detail of one module; when it's scattered, every caller is silently coupled to the DDL, and a migration becomes a 47-site refactor instead of a one-file edit.

repository-data-access-layer.title: A repository is the single gateway to one entity's storage
repository-data-access-layer.text: All access to an entity goes through one interface — findById, save, query-by-intent — that returns domain objects, never raw rows. The invariant: callers depend on the interface, never on the schema. Change the table, the index, the SQL — callers never know.

repository-data-access-layer.title: The repository as the only door to the orders table
repository-data-access-layer.subtitle: Three callers reach the Order entity through ONE OrderRepository interface. Schema, query plans, indexes, and the expand/contract migration all live behind the seam. Reporting reads a separate read-model and is deliberately out of scope.

source of truth

repository-data-access-layer.subtitle: An interface callers depend on + a Postgres implementation that owns the SQL, the mapping, and the transaction — so a column rename never leaks out.

steps.label: The interface IS the contract
steps.note: Callers import OrderRepository, never PgOrderRepository. Methods are phrased by INTENT (findByCustomer), not by SQL. No method takes a WHERE string or returns a raw row — that is what keeps the schema private.

steps.label: SQL lives in exactly one place

steps.label: save owns the transaction boundary
steps.note: BEGIN/COMMIT/ROLLBACK live in the repo, not the caller. Atomicity and isolation are the repository's responsibility — the upsert either fully lands or fully reverts.

steps.label: The mapping seam

repository-data-access-layer.caption: The repository converts a schema change from a cross-codebase coupling into a one-module edit with a defined rollback.

repository-data-access-layer.title: Expand / contract: the migration the repository makes safe
repository-data-access-layer.subtitle: The failure path (rename-in-place) breaks live readers mid-deploy. The repair path (expand → backfill → flip the repo → contract) keeps every caller working and gives a rollback at each step.

legend.label: rename-in-place: breaks live readers, no rollback
expand/contract: each step reversible
contract only after the new column is proven

repository-data-access-layer.text: The senior tell is reversibility, not cleverness. A rename-in-place migration is a one-way door — the instant you DROP the old column, every in-flight reader and your rollback plan die together. Expand/contract turns it into a two-way door: at every step both columns exist, the repository is the one switch that flips reads, and 'undo' is a flip-back, not a restore-from-backup.

repository-data-access-layer.question: A reviewer says: 'Prove this repository actually decouples callers from the schema — not just that it compiles.' What is the exact evidence?
options: The repository has findById, save, and findByCustomer methods with clean names.
A schema change (rename a column) ships behind the repo and the test suite passes with ZERO caller files modified — shown by the DDL diff plus an empty diff outside order-repository.ts.
The team agrees the repository pattern is a best practice.
The repository class is under 200 lines and well commented.
repository-data-access-layer.explanation: Decoupling is a property you demonstrate, not assert. The proof is a real migration whose blast radius stops at the repository: the DDL diff shows the column changed, and the code diff shows nothing outside the one implementation file moved — yet the suite still passes. Clean method names (1), consensus (3), and brevity (4) are happy-path signals; only the zero-caller-change migration falsifies 'the schema leaked'.

repository-data-access-layer.intro: Prove the repository holds — DDL diff, dry run, rollback, query plan, constraint test:
items: Grep the codebase for the table name (e.g. 'FROM orders'). If it appears outside the repository implementation, the abstraction leaks — every other hit is a caller coupled to the schema.
Run the rename as expand/contract against a dry-run/branch DB: capture the DDL diff, then confirm the app test suite passes with the only changed source file being the repository.
Keep the rollback script ready: flip the repo reads back to the old column and re-run — the system must return to a working state with no data loss.
Compare query plans before and after: EXPLAIN the repository's hot read on both column versions and confirm the index is still used (no accidental seq scan from the new column lacking an index).
Run the constraint test: assert NOT NULL / FK / unique constraints hold on the new column after backfill, so the contract step cannot drop the old column while data integrity is unproven.

prompts: Explain to a teammate why phrasing a repository method as findByCustomer (intent) instead of exposing a raw WHERE clause is what actually keeps the schema private.
Walk through your expand/contract migration and name the rollback action at each step — where exactly is the two-way door?
Point to the one place your column name appears in code, and explain why that single touch-point is the whole reason the rename didn't break 12 callers.

repository-data-access-layer.text: The seam is universal: anywhere callers would otherwise hard-code a storage shape, a repository absorbs the change. Swap Postgres for an in-memory fake in tests and your business logic runs with no DB; split the orders table into orders + order_lines and only the repository's SQL + mapping move; put a cache in front of findById and callers never know. What stays invariant is the interface and the intent-named methods; what changes is the implementation behind the seam — driven by scale, latency, or new integrity constraints. This same schema_migration_decision_and_rollback_packet.md is the artifact your database capstone reuses: it carries the DDL diff, the rollback script, the query-plan comparison, and the constraint test that prove a model can change under load without losing truth.

seed-fixtures-test-data.outcome: Take one real table (or a realistic one) and build a deterministic seed-fixture set: idempotent INSERTs that respect every constraint, a fixed reference time, and a teardown — proving a known data state a test can trust. Capture it in seed_fixtures_decision_and_rollback_packet.md.
seed-fixtures-test-data.proof: A runnable seed script + Section of seed_fixtures_decision_and_rollback_packet.md: the fixtures load on an empty schema, load AGAIN without error (idempotent), satisfy every FK and CHECK constraint, and a teardown returns the DB to empty. A reviewer runs it twice and the row counts are identical.
seed-fixtures-test-data.unlock: Your fixtures load idempotently inside a transaction, satisfy every constraint, pin a fixed clock, and tear down cleanly — a test reads the same state every run.
seed-fixtures-test-data.doNotClaim: Do not claim 'test data' if your seed uses NOW(), random IDs, or relies on insertion order for keys. That is non-deterministic data wearing a fixture's clothes — the test that depends on it is flaky by construction, and a flaky fixture is worse than none.

seed-fixtures-test-data.text: The suite is green on your laptop and red in CI — same code, same tests. The difference is the data: your local DB still holds yesterday's rows, and a fixture quietly assumed user id 7 already existed. A test that depends on leftover state is not a test; it is a coin flip.

Sitting in the production-pressure phase of Databases and Data Modeling, seed fixtures are the known, controlled data state every other database skill is verified against — migrations, query plans, constraint tests, and the capstone all stand on fixtures that say the same thing every run.

seed-fixtures-test-data.prompt: Your test inserts an order, then asserts the dashboard shows '1 order today'. It passes 100 times, then fails at midnight UTC. Why — before reading on?
seed-fixtures-test-data.reveal: The fixture used NOW() for the order timestamp, and 'today' rolled over mid-run. The data was never fixed — it drifted with the wall clock. A real fixture pins time: insert the order at a frozen reference instant ('2024-01-01 12:00:00Z') so 'today' is whatever YOU defined, not whatever the clock happened to read. Non-determinism in seed data is the #1 source of tests that pass until they don't.

seed-fixtures-test-data.title: A fixture is a deterministic, constraint-satisfying, idempotent known state
seed-fixtures-test-data.text: Seed fixtures pin every variable a test depends on: fixed IDs, a frozen clock, explicit values. The invariant: load twice, get the identical state; tear down, get empty. Same input rows, same DB, every run — or the test downstream is flaky.

seed-fixtures-test-data.title: The fixture lifecycle: failure path vs repair path
seed-fixtures-test-data.subtitle: Seed must satisfy constraints and be idempotent. The left branch (NOW(), duplicate key, FK violation) is the failure path; the repair path pins the clock, uses ON CONFLICT, and seeds parents before children.

edges.label: repair: pin clock · ON CONFLICT · parents first

legend.label: the seed step (the skill)
failure path — non-determinism / constraint break
repair path — deterministic known state

seed-fixtures-test-data.title: A deterministic seed, one line at a time
seed-fixtures-test-data.subtitle: fixtures/seed.sql — fixed IDs, frozen clock, idempotent, transactional, parents before children.

steps.label: Wrap in a transaction
steps.note: BEGIN/COMMIT makes the whole seed atomic: if any constraint fails, the DB rolls back to empty rather than half-loaded. Isolation means a parallel test never sees a partial fixture.

steps.label: Reset first → idempotency
steps.note: TRUNCATE ... RESTART IDENTITY CASCADE clears the tables and resets sequences so re-running yields the IDENTICAL state. This is what makes the seed safe to run twice.

steps.label: Fixed IDs + frozen clock
steps.note: Explicit ids (1,2) and a literal timestamp — never auto-increment-by-order or NOW(). The test can assert 'user 1' and '12:00:00' because YOU pinned them.

steps.label: ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING
steps.note: Belt-and-suspenders idempotency: even without the TRUNCATE, a second load won't raise a duplicate-key error. The UNIQUE constraint stays satisfied.

steps.label: Parents before children
steps.note: Orders carry a FK to users. Seed users first or every INSERT violates the foreign-key constraint. Insertion ORDER is part of the contract.

steps.label: Fast-forward the sequence
steps.note: After hand-setting IDs, bump the sequence past them so app-generated INSERTs don't collide with fixture IDs — a classic post-seed footgun.

seed-fixtures-test-data.caption: Run it, run it again — row counts identical, no errors. That repeatability IS the deliverable.

seed-fixtures-test-data.title: Weak fixture vs gold fixture
seed-fixtures-test-data.subtitle: Same goal — seed two users and their orders. Only one gives a test a state it can trust.

left.label: Weak: convenient, non-deterministic
lines: INSERT ... VALUES ('ada@...', NOW())  -- clock drifts
id auto-increments by insertion order
orders seeded before users → FK violation on a cold DB
second run → duplicate-key error (not idempotent)
no teardown → leftover rows leak into the next test
left.verdict: Passes locally, flaky in CI — a coin flip

right.label: Gold: deterministic known state
lines: fixed literal timestamp '2024-01-01T12:00:00Z'
explicit ids (1,2,10,11) — assertable, stable
parents (users) before children (orders) → FK-safe
TRUNCATE + ON CONFLICT → load twice, same state
transactional + teardown → empty after each test

seed-fixtures-test-data.caption: The gold version costs four extra lines (pin the clock, fix the IDs, order the inserts, reset) and buys a suite that never flakes on data.

seed-fixtures-test-data.symptom: Tests pass when run alone but fail when the suite runs in parallel: 'duplicate key value violates unique constraint users_email_key'. The fixture itself looks correct.
seed-fixtures-test-data.task: Two tests share this seed and both run it. Find why parallel runs collide, and fix it so the fixture is idempotent and isolated.
seed-fixtures-test-data.fix: The seed has no reset and no conflict handling, so the second test re-inserts id 1 and hits the UNIQUE constraint. Add `TRUNCATE orders, users RESTART IDENTITY CASCADE;` at the top (or `ON CONFLICT (id) DO NOTHING` on each INSERT) and a teardown after each test. Better: give each parallel worker its own transaction that ROLLBACKs at test end (isolation), so workers never share committed fixture rows at all.

seed-fixtures-test-data.text: The senior tell: fixtures live in version control next to the migration that shaped the schema, and the seed is re-derived whenever the schema changes — never hand-patched. SWEBOK V4 (data quality model in Software Quality; configuration management) and ACM/IEEE CS2023 support treating this as data-quality and change-control discipline: test data is an artifact with the same change-control as the schema it populates. (SWEBOK does not tie test data to schemas specifically; that framing is inference, not a stated standard.) A fixture that drifts from the current constraints is a silent lie your whole suite trusts.

seed-fixtures-test-data.question: A reviewer asks: 'Show me the exact evidence that these fixtures aren't just a happy-path INSERT.' Which response actually proves it?
options: 'The INSERTs all succeeded the first time I ran them.'
'I ran the seed on an empty schema, then ran it again — identical row counts, no error; I removed the user INSERT and the order INSERT failed the FK check; teardown returned the DB to zero rows.'
'The fixtures cover every column in the table.'
'I used realistic-looking names and emails for the rows.'
seed-fixtures-test-data.explanation: Proof is behavior under repetition and breakage, not a single green run. Option 2 demonstrates idempotency (run twice, same state), constraint enforcement (FK fails when the parent is missing), and clean teardown (back to empty) — the three properties that make a fixture trustworthy. Coverage (3) and plausible data (4) say nothing about determinism; a first-run success (1) is exactly the happy path the reviewer is challenging.

seed-fixtures-test-data.intro: Prove your fixtures hold — no vibes:
items: Run the seed on an empty schema, then run it again. If row counts differ or it errors on the second run, it is not idempotent — add TRUNCATE/RESTART IDENTITY or ON CONFLICT.
Grep the seed for NOW(), CURRENT_TIMESTAMP, and random IDs. Any dynamic value is non-determinism — replace it with a fixed literal.
Delete one parent row's INSERT and re-run: a child INSERT must fail the foreign-key constraint. If it doesn't, your FK is missing or deferred — the fixture isn't testing what you think.
Run the teardown and SELECT count(*) on every fixture table. Anything but zero means rows leak into the next test.
Run the suite twice in a row WITHOUT manually resetting the DB. If the second run fails, a test depends on leftover state, not on the fixture.

prompts: In your own words: why does a single NOW() in a seed quietly make an entire test suite flaky?
Explain idempotency for fixtures using your own seed — what makes running it twice safe, and what breaks if it isn't?
Why must parent rows be seeded before child rows, and which constraint enforces that? Use your own schema as the example.

seed-fixtures-test-data.text: The same discipline travels to any system that needs a known starting state: a payments test seeds a fixed customer + a fixed card token at a frozen clock; an analytics pipeline replays a canned event log so 'yesterday' is deterministic; a game integration test loads a saved board, not a random one. What stays invariant is determinism, constraint-satisfaction, idempotency, and teardown; what changes is the schema, the volume, and the privacy rules (production-like fixtures must use synthetic, not real, PII). Carry seed_fixtures_decision_and_rollback_packet.md into the database capstone — the migration dry-run, the query-plan comparison, and the constraint tests all run AGAINST these fixtures. The schema change you verify next module is only trustworthy because the data underneath it says the same thing every time.

data-quality-checks.outcome: Take one real (or realistic) table and write a Data Quality Checks suite: at least four falsifiable assertions over a known invariant — not-null on a required column, a uniqueness/key check, a referential check across a relationship, and a domain/range constraint — each phrased so a bad row makes it FAIL loudly, not pass quietly.
data-quality-checks.proof: The artifact data_quality_contract.sql attached to the evidence ledger: 4+ named checks, each with the invariant it guards, the exact failing row it would catch, and a run transcript showing it returns rows (FAIL) on dirty data and zero rows (PASS) on clean data. A reviewer can run it without you narrating.
data-quality-checks.unlock: Each check names an invariant, is falsifiable (a wrong row makes it fail), and you have a transcript proving it both passes on clean data and fails on a seeded bad row.
data-quality-checks.doNotClaim: Do not claim you 'have data quality checks' if every check returns zero rows because it can only ever pass. A check that cannot fail is decoration, not a check. Each assertion must be able to surface a violating row — and you must have seen it do so at least once.

data-quality-checks.text: The migration shipped green, the dashboard turned up, and three weeks later finance finds duplicate order_ids inflating revenue 4% — the constraint that would have caught it on row one was never written. Bad data does not announce itself; it compounds in silence until someone trusts a number that was never true.

This lesson opens Module 4 in the production-pressure phase: a schema change must preserve integrity while supporting a new query path and a rollback plan. A data quality check is the enforceable, falsifiable assertion that turns 'the data is probably fine' into Section 1 of the migration packet you carry through this module.

data-quality-checks.prompt: Your orders table has a NOT NULL constraint on customer_id and a foreign key to customers. Is your data quality already guaranteed? Answer before reading on.
data-quality-checks.reveal: No — constraints only enforce what they were declared on, going forward. They say nothing about rows that predate them, nothing about a customer_id that points to a soft-deleted customer, nothing about an amount of -$40, and nothing about the 6% of rows where status is 'shipped' but shipped_at is NULL. The schema enforces shape; data quality checks enforce truth. The gap between them is exactly where silent corruption lives.

data-quality-checks.title: A quality check is a falsifiable assertion over an invariant — it must be able to FAIL
data-quality-checks.text: Name the invariant (the thing that must always be true), write a query whose result is the set of rows that VIOLATE it, and assert that set is empty. The invariant: a check earns its place only if a bad row makes it fail loudly. A check that can only pass proves nothing.

data-quality-checks.title: Where checks sit on the write → store → trust path
data-quality-checks.subtitle: Six stages from ingest to a trusted query. Checks gate the load and run again post-migration; the failure path (silent bad rows reaching the dashboard) is what the quality contract exists to cut off.

data-quality-checks.title: Writing the quality contract, one check at a time
data-quality-checks.subtitle: data_quality_contract.sql — four falsifiable assertions; each SELECT returns the VIOLATING rows, so empty = PASS, any row = FAIL.
data-quality-checks.code:
-- data_quality_contract.sql  · invariant set for orders (run pre-promote AND post-migration)

-- CHECK 1 (completeness): every order must name a customer
SELECT id FROM orders WHERE customer_id IS NULL;

-- CHECK 2 (uniqueness): order_id is a key — no duplicates may exist
SELECT order_id, COUNT(*) FROM orders GROUP BY order_id HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;

-- CHECK 3 (referential): no order may point to a missing/soft-deleted customer
SELECT o.id FROM orders o
  LEFT JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id
  WHERE c.id IS NULL OR c.deleted_at IS NOT NULL;

-- CHECK 4 (domain): amount must be >= 0, and 'shipped' implies a shipped_at
SELECT id FROM orders
  WHERE amount < 0
     OR (status = 'shipped' AND shipped_at IS NULL);

-- PASS contract: all four queries return ZERO rows. Any returned row is a violation.

steps.label: The contract header
steps.note: One file, run at the same two moments every migration: before promoting staged rows, and again right after the schema change — the rollback plan keys off these results.

steps.label: Completeness check
steps.note: The query returns rows that VIOLATE the not-null invariant. Phrasing it as 'find the bad rows' is what makes it falsifiable — empty result = pass.

steps.label: Uniqueness check
steps.note: GROUP BY + HAVING COUNT(*) > 1 surfaces duplicate order_ids a UNIQUE constraint would have blocked on insert — but catches the ones already in the table from before the constraint existed.

steps.label: Referential check
steps.note: An FK alone won't catch a customer that was SOFT-deleted after the order was written. The LEFT JOIN finds orphans the constraint silently allows.

steps.label: Domain / range check
steps.note: Two invariants in one: amount can't be negative, and a 'shipped' status must have a timestamp. This is the state-consistency rule a column type can't express.

steps.label: The pass rule
steps.note: Empty across all four = PASS. This is the line that makes the file a contract: a reviewer runs it and reads the result, no narration needed.

data-quality-checks.caption: Seed one bad row per check (a NULL customer_id, a duplicate order_id, an orphan, a -$40 order) and confirm each query returns exactly that row before you trust the suite.

data-quality-checks.title: Two 'quality checks' on the same migration
data-quality-checks.subtitle: Both look like diligence in the PR. Only one can ever catch a bad row.

left.label: Vague reassurance
lines: 'I spot-checked the data, looks good'
Relies on existing NOT NULL / FK only (shape, not truth)
No query that returns violating rows
Never run against a seeded bad row
Can report 'pass' even when 6% of rows are wrong
left.verdict: Can only ever pass — proves nothing

right.label: Falsifiable contract
lines: 4 named checks: completeness, uniqueness, referential, domain
Each SELECT returns the rows that VIOLATE the invariant
Run pre-promote AND post-migration
Demonstrated FAIL on a seeded dirty row, then PASS on clean
Empty result is the proof; any row is a blocker
right.verdict: Can fail loudly — so passing means something

data-quality-checks.caption: The teaching signal: a check you have never seen fail is a check you cannot trust. Make it fail once on purpose before you rely on it passing.

data-quality-checks.symptom: The uniqueness check reports PASS on a table you KNOW has duplicate order_ids — finance found them last week.
data-quality-checks.brokenCode:
-- 'uniqueness' check
SELECT order_id FROM orders WHERE order_id IS NOT NULL;
data-quality-checks.task: This query can only ever pass (it returns every non-null order_id, which the author reads as 'they all exist'). Rewrite it so it returns ONLY the rows that violate the uniqueness invariant — and explain why the original is theater.
data-quality-checks.fix: SELECT order_id, COUNT(*) FROM orders GROUP BY order_id HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;  — The original checked presence, not uniqueness: 'is the column populated' instead of 'is the key actually unique'. A check must return the VIOLATING set (duplicates), so an empty result is the only thing that means PASS. The duplicate-key incident was invisible because the check could not express the invariant it claimed to guard.

data-quality-checks.text: Standards grounding (SWEBOK V4 Software Quality, which defines a general data quality model): the senior tell is treating a quality rule as an executable, falsifiable assertion versioned alongside the schema — not a paragraph in a runbook. (SWEBOK defines data-quality characteristics but does not prescribe executable assertions versioned with a schema; that specific practice is the author's, not the standard's.) If your check isn't a query you can run in CI and watch turn red, it isn't enforced; it's a hope. Run the contract pre-promote and again post-migration so the rollback decision keys off evidence, not vibes.

data-quality-checks.question: A reviewer asks for the exact evidence that your data quality checks aren't just happy-path answers. What do you point to?
options: The PR comment saying all checks returned zero rows.
A transcript showing each check returning the seeded violating row (FAIL) on dirty data and zero rows (PASS) after the fix — proving each assertion can fail.
The list of NOT NULL and FOREIGN KEY constraints already in the schema.
A note that the data 'looked correct' after the migration.
data-quality-checks.explanation: A check that has only ever returned zero rows might be enforcing nothing — you can't tell a real pass from a check that can't fail. The evidence is the demonstrated FAIL-then-PASS transcript: it proves the assertion is falsifiable AND that the violation it guards against is now absent. The schema constraints (3) cover shape going forward but not pre-existing or state-consistency invariants; 'looked correct' (4) is exactly the vibe this lesson kills.

data-quality-checks.intro: Prove your quality contract holds — no vibes:
items: Every check returns the VIOLATING rows, not the valid ones. If empty doesn't mean PASS, the polarity is backwards — fix it.
For each check, seed one bad row (NULL customer_id, duplicate order_id, orphan FK, negative amount) and confirm the check returns exactly that row. A check you've never seen fail is unproven.
At least one check reaches across a relationship (the referential/orphan check) — not just single-column shape an FK already enforces.
At least one check encodes a state-consistency invariant a column type can't express (e.g. status='shipped' implies shipped_at IS NOT NULL).
You ran the suite pre-promote AND post-migration, and the rollback condition is written against the results — a non-empty CHECK 2 or 3 blocks promotion.

prompts: In your own words: why does phrasing a check to return VIOLATING rows (instead of valid rows) make it falsifiable — and why does falsifiability matter more than the check passing?
Explain the gap between a schema constraint and a data quality check, using your orphan-FK check as the example: what does the FK miss that your check catches?
Which invariant in your contract is most likely to break under the next migration, and what exact row would prove it broke?

data-quality-checks.text: Not a SQL move — the move. A falsifiable assertion over an invariant transfers anywhere truth must survive change: a financial reconciliation check (debits must equal credits, return the rows where they don't), an API contract test (this field must never be null in the response), an ML pipeline guard (no feature outside its trained range). What stays invariant is the shape — name the rule, return the violators, assert empty, prove it can fail. What changes is the domain, the cost of a false negative, and how loud the failure must be. Next this exact contract becomes Section 1 of schema_migration_decision_and_rollback_packet.md: the database capstone reuses these checks as the pre/post-migration gate and the rollback trigger — if the artifact can't be reused there, the lesson isn't done.

backup-restore-retention.outcome: Take one real (or realistic) production database and write a Backup, Restore & Retention policy that proves recovery — not just that backups exist. Define the recovery objectives (RPO/RTO), a tested restore drill, and a retention schedule with a documented expiry, then attach it to the evidence ledger.
backup-restore-retention.proof: The `schema_migration_decision_and_rollback_packet.md` artifact gains a Backup/Restore/Retention section: stated RPO + RTO, a restore-drill transcript (backup → restore to a scratch instance → row-count + checksum match), and a retention schedule with a defended expiry. A reviewer can point to the restore transcript, not just the backup job's green checkmark.
backup-restore-retention.unlock: Your policy names an RPO and RTO, includes a transcript of an actually-executed restore that verified the data, and a retention schedule whose expiry you can defend.
backup-restore-retention.doNotClaim: Do not claim you have backups if you have never restored one. A backup that has never been restored is an untested hypothesis, not a recovery plan. The invariant of this skill is the restore, not the dump — 'the cron ran green' is theatre until a restore reproduces the data.

backup-restore-retention.text: The migration dropped a column at 2 a.m. and the rollback script had a typo, so the team reaches for last night's backup — and discovers the nightly dump has been silently writing a zero-byte file for three weeks. The backups existed. None of them restored.

Schema design, constraints, and migrations all assume the data underneath survives a bad change. Backup, Restore & Retention is the safety net that makes a destructive migration reversible — Section 5 of the same `schema_migration_decision_and_rollback_packet.md` you carry through this course, the part a reviewer trusts only when a restore has actually run.

backup-restore-retention.prompt: "We run a nightly pg_dump to S3 and the job is green." Before you call that a backup strategy — what is the unproven assumption hiding in it? Answer before reading on.
backup-restore-retention.reveal: Two assumptions, both untested: that the dump contains restorable data, and that you can restore it inside your recovery-time target. A green job proves a file was written, not that the file restores. The real invariant is RPO/RTO met by a *tested* restore: how much data you can lose (RPO) and how fast you can be back (RTO). Most 'backup outages' are restore failures — corrupt dumps, missing roles, an unrecoverable WAL gap — discovered for the first time during the incident.

backup-restore-retention.title: A backup policy is RPO + RTO + a tested restore + a defended retention
backup-restore-retention.text: Name how much data you may lose (RPO) and how fast you must recover (RTO), prove a restore actually reproduces the data, and set a retention schedule with a defended expiry. The invariant: the restore is the deliverable, never the dump.

backup-restore-retention.title: The backup → restore → retention loop, with both paths
backup-restore-retention.subtitle: A nightly base backup plus continuous WAL gives point-in-time recovery. The FAILURE path (corrupt or zero-byte dump) and the REPAIR path (restore drill catches it before the incident) are both on the map. The app's live primary is deliberately out of the restore target — you restore to scratch.

backup-restore-retention.title: The restore drill — the proof, line by line
backup-restore-retention.subtitle: A backup nobody restored is a hypothesis. This script restores last night's dump to a scratch database and verifies the data matches — the transcript IS the evidence.
backup-restore-retention.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

BACKUP="s3://db-backups/orders/$(date -d yesterday +%F).dump"
SCRATCH="orders_restore_check"
RPO_MAX_MIN=15   # we accept losing at most 15 min of writes
RTO_MAX_MIN=30   # we must be queryable again within 30 min

start=$(date +%s)
aws s3 cp "$BACKUP" /tmp/restore.dump
[ -s /tmp/restore.dump ] || { echo "FAIL: backup is zero-byte"; exit 1; }

dropdb --if-exists "$SCRATCH" && createdb "$SCRATCH"
pg_restore --no-owner --exit-on-error -d "$SCRATCH" /tmp/restore.dump

rows=$(psql -tAc "SELECT count(*) FROM orders" "$SCRATCH")
sum=$(psql -tAc "SELECT md5(string_agg(id::text, ',' ORDER BY id)) FROM orders" "$SCRATCH")
elapsed_min=$(( ($(date +%s) - start) / 60 ))

echo "restored rows=$rows checksum=$sum in ${elapsed_min}m"
[ "$elapsed_min" -le "$RTO_MAX_MIN" ] || { echo "FAIL: RTO ${elapsed_min}m > ${RTO_MAX_MIN}m"; exit 1; }
[ "$rows" -gt 0 ] || { echo "FAIL: restored table is empty"; exit 1; }
echo "PASS: RPO<=${RPO_MAX_MIN}m, RTO=${elapsed_min}m, data verified"

steps.label: Point at a REAL backup
steps.note: Yesterday's actual dump, not a fixture. If the drill never touches production artifacts, it proves nothing about production recovery.

steps.label: Declare RPO and RTO as numbers
steps.note: RPO = max acceptable data loss (15 min). RTO = max acceptable downtime (30 min). These are the contract the restore must satisfy — a backup with no objectives can't pass or fail.

steps.label: Catch the zero-byte failure first
steps.note: `-s` fails on an empty file — the exact silent failure from the mission. The cheapest disqualifier runs before the expensive restore.

steps.label: Restore to SCRATCH, never the primary
steps.note: `--exit-on-error` makes a partial restore a failure, not a warning. You restore to a throwaway DB so the drill is safe to run on a schedule.

steps.label: Verify the DATA, not just exit code 0
steps.note: Row count plus a content checksum. A restore can exit 0 and still hand you an empty or truncated table — the checksum is what turns 'it ran' into 'the data is there'.

steps.label: Assert against RTO, then PASS
steps.note: If the restore blew the 30-minute budget, it FAILS even with correct data — slow recovery is a failed recovery during an outage. The PASS line is the transcript you attach to the packet.

backup-restore-retention.caption: Run this on a schedule and the zero-byte failure surfaces on a quiet Tuesday, not at 2 a.m. mid-incident. The PASS transcript is the reviewable artifact.

backup-restore-retention.title: "We have backups" vs a tested recovery policy
backup-restore-retention.subtitle: Same nightly job, same S3 bucket. Only one survives the incident in the mission.

left.label: Backups exist (untested)
lines: Nightly pg_dump → S3, cron is green
No RPO/RTO — 'we'll restore if we need to'
Never once restored a dump
Retention = 'keep everything' (cost creeps, GDPR risk)
Zero-byte dumps go unnoticed for weeks
left.verdict: Recovery is an untested hypothesis

right.label: Tested recovery policy
lines: RPO=15m (base + WAL), RTO=30m, both stated
Scheduled restore drill to scratch + checksum verify
Last PASS transcript attached to the packet
Retention: 7 daily / 4 weekly / 12 monthly, expiry defended
Zero-byte / corrupt dump fails the drill, not the incident
right.verdict: Recovery is proven and reversible

backup-restore-retention.caption: The difference is one executed restore. A green backup job tells you a file was written; a PASS transcript tells you production can come back — and within your time budget.

backup-restore-retention.text: The senior tell on a backup review is not 'do you have backups' — everyone says yes. It's 'when did you last restore one, and how long did it take?' Anchored to ACM/IEEE CS2023's data-management competency: a recovery capability you have never exercised is indistinguishable from no recovery capability. Schedule the restore drill so the answer is always 'last week, in 22 minutes,' not 'we'd have to check.'

backup-restore-retention.question: A reviewer says: "Show me the exact evidence that this isn't just a happy-path answer." Which proves your backup policy is real?
options: A screenshot of the nightly backup cron job showing a green checkmark for the last 30 days.
A transcript of a restore drill: a real backup restored to a scratch DB, row count and checksum matching, completed inside the stated RTO.
A list of every backup file in the S3 bucket with their sizes and timestamps.
A note in the runbook saying 'backups are configured and monitored.'
backup-restore-retention.explanation: Only option 2 proves recovery. The green cron (1) and the file list (3) prove dumps were *written* — the exact thing that was true in the mission while every dump was zero bytes. A runbook note (4) is an assertion, not evidence. The restore transcript is the only artifact that demonstrates the data comes back, intact, within RTO — the invariant of this skill.

backup-restore-retention.intro: Prove your policy recovers — no green-checkmark theatre:
items: State your RPO and RTO as numbers, not adjectives. 'Recent' and 'fast' are not objectives — '15 minutes of loss, 30 minutes to recover' are.
Point to a restore transcript from an ACTUAL run: a backup restored to a scratch instance with row count and a content checksum that match the source.
Confirm the drill catches the silent failure: feed it a zero-byte or truncated dump and verify it FAILS rather than passing.
Confirm the restore completed inside your stated RTO. If it didn't, the RTO is aspirational — either fix the restore or revise the number honestly.
Defend your retention expiry: name what you keep, for how long, and why deleting older copies is safe (cost + privacy/GDPR pressure vs. the RPO window you must preserve).

prompts: In your own words: why is a backup that has never been restored an untested hypothesis rather than a recovery plan? Use your own policy as the example.
Explain RPO vs RTO to a junior using your numbers — how much data you can lose vs how fast you must be back — and how each one shaped a decision in your policy.
Defend your retention expiry: which copy did you choose to delete, and how do you know deleting it doesn't drop you below your RPO window?

backup-restore-retention.text: The pattern is domain-independent: a capability you've never exercised under realistic conditions is a capability you don't have. A pilot rehearses engine-out in the simulator before the real failure; an ops team runs game-day chaos drills before the real outage; you run a restore drill before the real data loss. Same move — prove recovery on a quiet day so it isn't your first attempt during the incident. This Backup/Restore/Retention section completes the `schema_migration_decision_and_rollback_packet.md`: the capstone reuses it directly, because a destructive migration is only reversible if a tested restore stands behind the rollback script. If the artifact can't be reused there, the lesson isn't done.

security-privacy-compliance.outcome: Take one table that holds PII (users, with email, name, ssn_last4, marketing_consent) and write the Security & Privacy section of schema_migration_decision_and_rollback_packet.md: the threat you defend, the access constraint enforced IN the database (row-level security + least-privilege role), the encryption boundary for the sensitive column, and the GDPR-correct deletion path — with a rollback that cannot leak.
security-privacy-compliance.proof: The Security & Privacy section of schema_migration_decision_and_rollback_packet.md: a named threat, an RLS policy that the app role cannot bypass, one column moved behind an encryption boundary, a deletion path that satisfies erasure WITHOUT breaking referential integrity, and a rollback script proven not to re-expose deleted PII. A reviewer with the app credentials runs SELECT and cannot read another tenant's rows.
security-privacy-compliance.unlock: Your packet enforces access in the database (not just the app), names the encryption boundary, and proves the deletion + rollback path cannot re-expose PII.
security-privacy-compliance.doNotClaim: Do not claim the data is 'secured' because the application checks permissions. App-layer checks are bypassed the moment anyone connects with the same DB credentials — a script, a BI tool, a leaked connection string. If the constraint is not enforced by the database, you have a convention, not a control.

security-privacy-compliance.text: A regulator's letter arrives: a user invoked their right to erasure 40 days ago and just found their data still queryable in your analytics replica. The DELETE ran — but a foreign key from orders silently soft-failed, the row survived in a backup snapshot, and a nightly job restored it. One missing constraint became a reportable breach.

Security, privacy, and compliance are not a layer you bolt on after the schema works — they are invariants the schema must hold under change, load, and bad input. This lesson turns 'we should protect PII' into a reviewable migration packet that enforces access, encryption, and erasure inside the database itself.

security-privacy-compliance.prompt: Your app code carefully checks `if (user.tenant_id === row.tenant_id)` before returning every row. Is the tenant's data isolated? Answer before reading on.
security-privacy-compliance.reveal: No — it is isolated only as long as every query in the company forever routes through that one code path. The analytics job, the data-science notebook, the on-call engineer's psql session, and the next teammate's new endpoint all connect with the same database role and see every tenant's rows. Isolation that lives in application code is a promise; isolation that lives in a row-level-security policy on the table is a control. The database, not the app, has to refuse the read.

security-privacy-compliance.title: Push the control down to the data, and make erasure a first-class path
security-privacy-compliance.text: Enforce access with database row-level security under a least-privilege role; put sensitive columns behind an encryption boundary; design deletion to satisfy erasure without orphaning rows or surviving in backups. The invariant: every privacy control holds even when the application is bypassed.

security-privacy-compliance.title: Where the PII control actually lives
security-privacy-compliance.subtitle: A read request and an erasure request hitting the same users table. The app-layer check is a convenience; the enforced control is the RLS policy + least-privilege role at the store. The replica and backup are the leak paths erasure must reach. Billing is out of scope.

legend.label: the enforced control (RLS + role)
leak paths erasure must reach
convenience / out of scope

security-privacy-compliance.title: The migration that enforces the controls
security-privacy-compliance.subtitle: schema_migration_decision_and_rollback_packet — the DDL that makes privacy an invariant of the table, not a habit of the app.

steps.label: Encryption boundary
steps.note: ssn_last4 moves into a bytea encrypted with a key the DB never stores in plaintext. The migration is a transaction — if encryption fails mid-table, the whole step rolls back and no half-encrypted state ships.

steps.label: FORCE, not just ENABLE
steps.note: ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY leaves the table OWNER exempt — the most common silent hole. FORCE makes the policy apply to everyone, so a migration role or a superuser-adjacent connection cannot quietly read across tenants.

steps.label: The isolation constraint
steps.note: The policy IS the control: a row is invisible unless its tenant_id matches the session's tenant. This holds for psql, BI tools, and next quarter's new endpoint — none of them can opt out.

steps.label: Least privilege
steps.note: app_rw gets DML, never DDL. A compromised app credential cannot DROP the policy or ALTER the table to disable RLS.

steps.label: Partial index on live rows
steps.note: Indexing WHERE deleted_at IS NULL keeps the hot path fast AND keeps tombstoned (erased) rows out of the index that feeds normal queries — privacy and performance from one constraint.

steps.label: Erasure without orphans
steps.note: Erase by nulling PII + tombstoning, NOT hard DELETE — orders.user_id keeps a valid FK target, so referential integrity survives while the personal data is gone. SECURITY DEFINER runs it under a controlled role.

security-privacy-compliance.caption: Run as the app_rw role: SELECT returns only your tenant; ssn_last4 is unreadable without the key; erase_user leaves a referentially-valid, PII-free skeleton.

security-privacy-compliance.title: App-enforced privacy vs database-enforced privacy
security-privacy-compliance.subtitle: Same users table, same erasure requirement. One is a convention every future query must remember; one is an invariant the data enforces.

left.label: App-layer convention
lines: Tenant check lives in one service's code
ssn_last4 stored as plaintext column
Erasure = hard DELETE users WHERE id=...
DELETE soft-fails on orders FK → row survives
No FORCE RLS: analytics replica sees all tenants
Backup snapshot still holds the 'deleted' PII
left.verdict: A psql session or a backup restore re-exposes everything

right.label: Database-enforced control
lines: FORCE row-level security on the table itself
ssn_last4 behind an encryption boundary
Erasure = null PII + tombstone, FK skeleton kept
Referential integrity survives erasure
least-privilege role can't disable the policy
Erasure path documented to reach replica + backups
right.verdict: Bypassing the app changes nothing — the data refuses

security-privacy-compliance.caption: The test: hand a reviewer the app credentials and a raw psql prompt. The right column survives it; the left column is a breach waiting for the first query that forgets the check.

security-privacy-compliance.text: Standards grounding: GDPR Art. 17 (erasure) and Art. 32 (security of processing) both demand the control be effective, not merely intended — which is why reviewers look for FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY, not ENABLE. ENABLE leaves the table owner exempt, so a single migration connection or admin tool quietly defeats your tenant isolation. The senior tell on a privacy migration is that the author can name who is still exempt from the policy — and has closed that gap on purpose. (SWEBOK V4 Software Security; ABET Computing Outcomes.)

security-privacy-compliance.question: A reviewer says: 'Show me the exact evidence this isolation isn't just a happy-path app check.' Which response actually proves it?
options: The service has unit tests confirming it filters rows by tenant_id before returning them.

Connecting directly as the app_rw role in psql, SELECT * FROM users returns only the current tenant's rows because FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY applies the tenant_isolation policy, and app_rw lacks DDL to disable it.
The ORM is configured to always add a WHERE tenant_id clause to generated queries.
Access to the production database is restricted to three engineers.
security-privacy-compliance.explanation: Only option 2 proves the control lives in the database and survives bypassing the app: FORCE RLS applies the policy to the very role the app uses, and the least-privilege grant means that role can't turn it off. App unit tests (1) and ORM clauses (3) both evaporate the moment any other query path touches the table; restricting human access (4) does nothing against an automated job or a leaked credential using app_rw.

security-privacy-compliance.intro: Prove the packet's controls hold — no vibes:
items: Connect as app_rw in raw psql (not through the app) and SELECT across tenants — you must see only your own tenant's rows. If you see others, RLS is ENABLEd but not FORCEd, or the role is exempt.
Run a DDL diff of the migration and confirm the plaintext PII column is DROPped, not just shadowed — grep the up-migration for the old column name.
Dry-run the migration in a transaction and ROLLBACK; confirm the table is byte-identical to before (no half-encrypted rows, no lingering policy).
Call erase_user on a row that has child orders, then check the orders FK still resolves AND email/name/ssn are NULL — erasure must not orphan and must not leave PII.
Trace the erasure to its leak paths: name how the tombstone reaches the analytics replica and how it ages out of backup snapshots. An erasure that stops at the primary is not GDPR-complete.

prompts: Explain why FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY changes the security model versus plain ENABLE, using who is exempt in each case.
Walk through erase_user: why is tombstone-and-null the right erasure here instead of a hard DELETE, in terms of referential integrity and the orders foreign key?
Your rollback re-adds the dropped column. Explain how you ensure the rollback does NOT restore PII that a user already erased — what does the rollback have to check first?

security-privacy-compliance.text: The pattern is domain-independent: push the privacy control down to where the data lives, and make erasure a designed path with a non-leaking rollback. A healthcare schema swaps tenant isolation for HIPAA minimum-necessary access and encrypts diagnosis codes; a payments schema keeps the PCI cardholder boundary out of the main table entirely and tokenizes. What stays invariant: the control is enforced by the database, the sensitive column has a named encryption boundary, and erasure reaches every replica and backup. What changes is the regulation, the column, and the blast radius. This same schema_migration_decision_and_rollback_packet.md is the artifact your database capstone reuses — its RLS policy, DDL diff, and erasure proof are exactly what the capstone's reviewer signs off on.

caching-read-models.outcome: Take one read-heavy query that is straining your source-of-truth tables and design a cached read model for it — then write the decision-and-rollback packet that names the staleness contract, the invalidation trigger, and the consistency you are trading away.
caching-read-models.proof: Section 'Caching Read Models' of schema_migration_decision_and_rollback_packet.md: the chosen read model, the bounded staleness window, the invalidation path (event or TTL), the rejected option, the expected failure, and a query-plan before/after. A reviewer agrees the cache can go stale safely and recover without serving wrong totals as if they were authoritative.
caching-read-models.unlock: Your read model names a bounded staleness contract, a concrete invalidation trigger, and the consistency guarantee it gives up — with the source of truth still recoverable.
caching-read-models.doNotClaim: Do not claim you have 'cached the read model' if you cannot say how stale a served row may be or what invalidates it. A cache with no staleness bound and no invalidation trigger is not a read model — it is silent data corruption with good latency.

caching-read-models.text: The dashboard 'Total Revenue' tile loads in 40 ms and everyone loves it — until finance notices it has read $2.1M for six hours while three refunds and a chargeback landed in Postgres. The number was fast, authoritative-looking, and wrong, because nobody wrote down when the cache was allowed to lie.

A read model is a precomputed, query-shaped copy of data that exists so a hot read path never re-derives the same aggregate against your normalized tables under load. It sits in the synthesis phase of this course because it only works once you can reason about the source schema, its constraints, and the transaction that keeps the cache and the truth from drifting apart.

caching-read-models.prompt: Your orders dashboard is slow, so you add a `dashboard_totals` table that stores the precomputed revenue per day. What is the one question that decides whether this is a read model or a future incident? Answer before reading on.
caching-read-models.reveal: Not 'is it faster' — it is 'when this row disagrees with the orders table, who wins and how does it heal?' A read model is a denormalized copy, so it WILL drift from the source of truth the moment a write lands and the copy lags. The skill is not building the cache; it is naming the staleness window the business accepts and the invalidation trigger that closes it. Without those two, you have not cached a read model — you have forked the truth and lost the fork.

caching-read-models.title: A read model is a derived copy bound by a staleness contract and an invalidation trigger
caching-read-models.text: Precompute the query-shaped result, keep Postgres as the source of truth, and write down two things: how stale a served row may be, and what re-derives it (event or TTL). The invariant: the cache may lag, never contradict, and always heals back to the source.

caching-read-models.title: The write → invalidate → read path of a cached read model
caching-read-models.subtitle: Postgres stays the source of truth. The Orders write fires an invalidation that re-derives the read model; the dashboard reads the model, never the raw tables. The failure path (stale read served as authoritative) and the repair path (event-driven rebuild) are both on the map.
