caching-read-models.title: The read model + its invalidation, end to end
caching-read-models.subtitle: A materialized daily_revenue read model, an event trigger that invalidates it on commit, and the bounded-staleness rebuild — the worked artifact behind the packet.
caching-read-models.code:
-- 1. The read model: a query-shaped, derived copy (NOT the source of truth)
CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW daily_revenue AS
SELECT order_date,
       SUM(amount_cents) AS revenue_cents,
       COUNT(*)         AS order_count,
       now()            AS derived_at
FROM orders
WHERE status = 'settled'
GROUP BY order_date;

CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ON daily_revenue (order_date);  -- enables CONCURRENT refresh

-- 2. Staleness contract: a served row may lag the orders table by <= 60s.
--    The dashboard reads daily_revenue, never SUM(orders) live.

-- 3. Invalidation trigger: every settled write enqueues a refresh.
CREATE FUNCTION enqueue_revenue_refresh() RETURNS trigger AS $$
BEGIN
  INSERT INTO refresh_queue(model, order_date) VALUES ('daily_revenue', NEW.order_date)
  ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING;          -- coalesce a burst into one rebuild
  RETURN NEW;
END; $$ LANGUAGE plpgsql;

CREATE TRIGGER orders_settled_refresh
  AFTER INSERT OR UPDATE OF status, amount_cents ON orders
  FOR EACH ROW WHEN (NEW.status = 'settled')
  EXECUTE FUNCTION enqueue_revenue_refresh();

-- 4. Rebuild (worker, off the read path): heals the copy back to the source.
REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY daily_revenue;  -- no read lock

steps.label: The derived copy
steps.note: daily_revenue is a precomputed aggregate of orders. It is a COPY — orders stays the source of truth. derived_at stamps how fresh each row is, so staleness is measurable, not a vibe.

steps.label: Unique index = concurrent refresh
steps.note: Without a unique index, REFRESH ... CONCURRENTLY is illegal and you must take a read lock. This one line is the difference between a rebuild that blocks the dashboard and one that doesn't.

steps.label: The staleness contract
steps.note: Write the bound down: a served row may lag by <= 60s. This is the consistency you are trading for latency — name it so finance can sign it, not discover it.

steps.label: Invalidation on commit
steps.note: Every settled write enqueues a refresh keyed by order_date. ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING coalesces a burst of refunds into one rebuild — the invalidation trigger the cache lives or dies by.

steps.label: Scoped, conditional trigger
steps.note: Fires only on status='settled' writes — not on every column update. A trigger that fires on everything turns your write path into a refresh storm.

steps.label: Rebuild heals back to truth
steps.note: CONCURRENTLY rebuilds off the read path with no read lock. This is the repair path on the diagram: the copy reconciles to Postgres, closing the staleness window.

caching-read-models.caption: A reviewer should trace a refund: it hits orders (truth), fires the trigger (invalidate), the worker refreshes CONCURRENTLY (heal), and the dashboard reads a row no more than 60s stale — never SUM(orders) live.

caching-read-models.subtitle: Same goal: stop SUM(orders) on every page load. Only one can go stale safely and recover.

caching-read-models.caption: A read model is allowed to be stale; it is never allowed to be wrong forever. The contract + invalidation trigger is what turns 'stale' into 'bounded and self-healing'.

caching-read-models.text: The senior tell: they design the cache MISS, not the cache hit. Anyone can serve the precomputed row. The judgment is in what happens when the read model is missing, mid-rebuild, or past its staleness bound — do you serve stale-but-flagged, fall back to the source query, or fail closed? SWEBOK V4's data-quality (Software Quality) and operability (Software Engineering Operations) axes support this: a read model without a defined behavior on staleness and on rebuild failure has no recovery story, and a cache with no recovery story is a future incident wearing a latency win. (SWEBOK does not discuss caches or read models specifically; the mapping is inference.)

caching-read-models.question: You add a materialized read model for a dashboard total. Which fact most determines whether it is production-safe rather than a silent-corruption risk?
options: It returns in under 50ms on the read path.
It defines a bounded staleness window AND an invalidation trigger that re-derives it from the source of truth, so it can lag but always reconciles.
It is stored in a faster engine than Postgres.
It precomputes every aggregate the dashboard might ever need.
caching-read-models.explanation: A read model is a derived copy, so drift from the source is guaranteed, not hypothetical. Safety comes from a named staleness bound plus an invalidation/rebuild trigger that reconciles the copy back to truth — that is what makes 'stale' mean 'bounded and self-healing' instead of 'silently wrong'. Latency (1), engine choice (3), and coverage (4) are real but secondary; none of them stop the cache from contradicting the source forever.

caching-read-models.intro: Prove your read model is safe — no vibes:
items: State the staleness bound out loud (e.g. '<= 60s'). If you cannot put a number on how old a served row may be, you have an uncontracted cache — fix it before shipping.
Name the invalidation trigger and trace one write through it: a refund hits orders, then WHAT fires the rebuild? If the answer is 'a person remembers to', it is not a trigger.
Run EXPLAIN on the dashboard query before and after: confirm it now reads the read model (index scan on daily_revenue), not a Seq Scan + aggregate over orders.
Force a rebuild failure (kill the worker) and confirm a defined behavior on staleness — stale-but-flagged, fallback, or fail-closed — not a silent old number.
Confirm the source of truth is untouched: you can DROP the read model and rebuild it from orders with zero data loss. If you can't, you cached the truth instead of deriving from it.

prompts: In your own words: why does a read model with no staleness bound and no invalidation trigger count as data corruption rather than caching?
Explain the difference between 'the cache may lag' and 'the cache may contradict', using your daily_revenue model as the example.
Walk a refund through your invalidation path out loud — write, trigger, rebuild, served row — and name the exact moment the staleness window opens and closes.

caching-read-models.text: The pattern is domain-independent: any time a read is hot and a derivation is expensive, you precompute a query-shaped copy and bind it with a staleness contract plus an invalidation trigger. A social feed caches a follower's timeline and invalidates on new posts; a billing system caches account balances and rebuilds on each ledger entry; a search index (the same write → index → read lag you mapped earlier in this course) IS a read model whose staleness is the indexing delay. What stays invariant is the discipline — source of truth, bounded lag, a trigger that heals the copy. What changes is the bound and the trigger, set by how much staleness the business can survive. This artifact, schema_migration_decision_and_rollback_packet.md, carries straight into the database capstone: the same packet that justifies the read model also carries the DDL diff, the rollback to drop it, and the query-plan proof that the read path actually moved off the source tables.

analytics-warehouse-boundaries.outcome: Take one operational table that an analytics team wants to query, and write the Boundary section of schema_migration_decision_and_rollback_packet.md: where the OLTP source of truth ends, where the warehouse begins, what crosses the boundary (and what must NOT), and the rollback if the new query path corrupts integrity.
analytics-warehouse-boundaries.proof: The Boundary + Decision + Rollback sections of schema_migration_decision_and_rollback_packet.md: the source-of-truth table named, the directed sync edge (OLTP -> warehouse) marked as one-way, the constraint that is NOT allowed to be enforced in the warehouse, the PII column held back, and a rollback script that drops the new read path without touching the operational schema. A reviewer can trace one row from write to dashboard and name exactly where truth lives.
analytics-warehouse-boundaries.unlock: Your packet names the source of truth, marks the sync as one-directional, lists what does NOT cross the boundary, and the rollback leaves the OLTP schema byte-for-byte unchanged.
analytics-warehouse-boundaries.doNotClaim: Do not claim you have 'set a warehouse boundary' if analytics queries hit the live OLTP tables directly, or if the warehouse can write back into the operational store. A shared table queried by both sides is not a boundary; it is a collision waiting for a long-running analytical scan to lock your checkout path.

analytics-warehouse-boundaries.text: A data analyst runs one innocent SELECT ... GROUP BY over the live orders table to build a quarterly chart; the unindexed full scan takes a row-level lock path, checkout latency spikes to 9 seconds, and the on-call gets paged for an outage that was really a missing boundary.

This is the synthesis lesson where schema, constraints, indexes, transactions, query plans, and privacy all collide at one seam: the line between the operational store that must stay correct under load and the analytics warehouse that must stay flexible for questions. Get the boundary wrong and analytics either corrupts truth or takes the transactional system down with it.

analytics-warehouse-boundaries.prompt: Your warehouse is a copy of production tables. To keep reports accurate, should you also copy the OLTP foreign-key and unique constraints into the warehouse? Decide before reading on.
analytics-warehouse-boundaries.reveal: No -- and that 'oh' is the boundary. A warehouse is a derived, denormalized, append-friendly read model; enforcing OLTP constraints there fights its job. A late-arriving fact or a soft-deleted dimension row will violate a foreign key and reject good analytical data. The warehouse trusts the source of truth UPSTREAM; it does not re-litigate integrity downstream. Constraints live where writes are authoritative -- the OLTP side -- not where you only read.

analytics-warehouse-boundaries.title: The warehouse is a one-way derived read model -- never the source of truth
analytics-warehouse-boundaries.text: The boundary is a contract: OLTP owns writes and integrity; the warehouse is an eventually-consistent, denormalized copy fed one direction only. The invariant -- truth flows source -> warehouse, never back, and analytical load never touches the operational tables.

analytics-warehouse-boundaries.title: The analytics warehouse boundary
analytics-warehouse-boundaries.subtitle: Five components across the write -> sync -> read seam. The one-way sync edge (Orders DB -> Warehouse) is the boundary; PII is held back; the dashboard reads the warehouse, never the OLTP store. A direct analyst-to-OLTP query is the failure path, drawn dashed.

analytics-warehouse-boundaries.title: Writing the Boundary + Rollback section, one line at a time
analytics-warehouse-boundaries.subtitle: schema_migration_decision_and_rollback_packet.md -- the migration that creates the read path AND its reversal.

steps.label: Name the boundary explicitly
steps.note: Source-of-truth table (orders) -> derived fact (analytics.fct_orders), sync direction stated. This one comment is the contract a reviewer signs.

steps.label: No re-enforced integrity
steps.note: order_id is NOT unique in the warehouse: CDC can deliver a row twice on replay, and an analytical model tolerates de-dup downstream. A UNIQUE here would reject good data.

steps.label: PII held back at the boundary
steps.note: The raw email never crosses; the sync masks it to customer_hash. Privacy is a property of the boundary, not an afterthought in a later GDPR ticket.

steps.label: Index for the QUERY PLAN, not the write
steps.note: ordered_at index serves the dashboard's time-range scans. The OLTP side stays lean; the analytical index lives only in the warehouse.

steps.label: Rollback touches only the warehouse
steps.note: DROP the fact table and its index -- the OLTP orders schema is never named in the reversal. That is the proof the boundary held: you can undo analytics without risking transactions.

steps.label: The reversal condition
steps.note: A concrete trigger (>0.5% row divergence for 30 min) -- not 'if it feels wrong'. Eventual consistency means you define how much drift is a bug.

analytics-warehouse-boundaries.caption: A peer should trace one order from the ACID write, through the one-way CDC load, into fct_orders -- and confirm the rollback cannot corrupt checkout.

analytics-warehouse-boundaries.text: The senior tell is which side owns the constraint. Constraints (foreign keys, unique, NOT NULL) belong where writes are authoritative -- the OLTP source of truth. In the warehouse you VALIDATE with tests and tolerances, you do not ENFORCE with constraints, because a late or replayed fact must be allowed to land. Grounding: ACM/IEEE CS2023's Data Management knowledge area treats data integrity and separates transactional consistency from analytical derivation. (SWEBOK V4 has no data-management KA and does not treat 'data integrity as a property of the system of record'; drop the SWEBOK attribution.) (References ground coverage; they are not endorsements.)

analytics-warehouse-boundaries.question: A reviewer asks: 'Show me the exact evidence this is a real boundary, not just two databases.' Which artifact proves it?
options: A screenshot of the dashboard rendering correctly with current numbers.
The rollback script drops only the warehouse fact table + index and never references the OLTP orders schema, plus a query-plan diff showing analytics no longer scans the live orders table.
A note saying 'analytics runs on a separate server now.'
A migration that adds the same UNIQUE and foreign-key constraints to the warehouse so the data matches production exactly.
analytics-warehouse-boundaries.explanation: The boundary is proven by what the rollback CANNOT touch (option 2): if reversing analytics never names the OLTP schema, the seam is real and one-way. A passing dashboard (1) shows the happy path only; 'separate server' (3) is infrastructure, not a contract; mirroring constraints (4) violates the boundary -- the warehouse re-litigating integrity is exactly the anti-pattern that rejects late-arriving facts.

CDC syncs one direction; no write-back path exists

analytics-warehouse-boundaries.caption: Source of truth on one side, derived read model on the other, one-way arrow between -- and a rollback that proves the seam by what it cannot reach.

analytics-warehouse-boundaries.intro: Prove the boundary holds -- no vibes:
items: Name the single source of truth for each fact. If two systems both claim to own writes for the same row, you have no boundary -- pick one.
Confirm the sync is one-directional: search the migration for any write path from warehouse back into OLTP. If one exists, the seam is broken.
Run EXPLAIN on the analyst's query: it must hit the warehouse fact table, not the live orders table. A plan that scans the OLTP source is a boundary leak.
Check no OLTP constraint (UNIQUE, foreign key) is re-enforced in the warehouse; verify a deliberately duplicated/late fact still loads instead of being rejected.
Confirm PII columns are masked or dropped at the boundary, not carried raw into the warehouse where every analyst can read them.
Execute the rollback in a dry run: it must drop only warehouse objects and leave the OLTP schema diff empty.

prompts: Explain why re-enforcing the OLTP unique constraint in the warehouse would reject good analytical data, using your own fct_orders table.
Trace one order from the ACID write to the dashboard, naming the one-way sync edge and exactly where truth lives.
Your rollback drops the warehouse fact table but never names the orders schema. Explain why that absence IS the proof the boundary is real.

analytics-warehouse-boundaries.text: The same boundary governs any 'system of record vs derived view' split: a search index is a one-way derived copy of the product catalog (you reindex from the DB, you never treat the index as truth); a read replica, a materialized view, a cache, an event-sourced projection -- all the same invariant. What stays fixed: one authoritative writer, one-way derivation, constraints at the source, tolerances downstream. What changes with scale, privacy, and latency: how fresh the copy must be and how much PII may cross. This packet -- schema_migration_decision_and_rollback_packet.md -- is your capstone evidence: not 'I understand warehouses' but 'here is a migration whose rollback proves analytics cannot corrupt the source of truth.' Carry it into the database capstone, where it joins the schema, migration, query-plan, quality, and backup proofs.

observability-incidents.outcome: Take one real (or realistic) database incident and write Section 1 of the packet: the incident framed against an SLO, the three signals you would inspect (a metric, a log/trace, a query plan), and the one observability gap that would have caught it earlier — then attach a rollback trigger.
observability-incidents.proof: Section 1 ("Incident Frame + Signals") of schema_migration_decision_and_rollback_packet.md: an SLO-anchored symptom (p99 vs target, error %, replication lag), three named evidence sources you actually checked, the missing instrumentation, and a concrete rollback trigger. A reviewer can replay your diagnosis from the signals alone, without you narrating.
observability-incidents.unlock: Your frame names an SLO breach (not a vibe), three real signals across layers (metric · log/trace · query plan), the observability gap, and a rollback trigger.
observability-incidents.doNotClaim: Do not claim you "observed" an incident if your evidence is one dashboard screenshot of CPU. CPU is a symptom, not a diagnosis. Observability means a metric points you, a log/trace explains, and a query plan confirms WHY the database did the slow thing. One number is monitoring; the three-layer trail is observability.

observability-incidents.text: 2:14 a.m.: checkout p99 jumps from 200ms to 9s, the orders table is fine on CPU, and three engineers are arguing about adding read replicas — until the on-call pulls one slow-query log line, runs EXPLAIN, and sees last night's migration silently dropped the index a seq-scan now eats. The fix is a rollback, not replicas. The difference was a signal trail, not a hunch.

This synthesis lesson connects everything earlier in the course — schema, constraints, indexes, migrations, transactions, query plans — to the moment they fail in production at 2 a.m. Observability is how a data model proves it still preserves truth under change and load: metrics point, logs and traces explain, and the query plan confirms the cause inside the database itself.

observability-incidents.prompt: Checkout latency spiked right after a deploy. The dashboard shows database CPU at 95%. Your teammate says "the DB is overloaded, add a replica." Before you agree — what is wrong with that diagnosis? Answer before reading on.
observability-incidents.reveal: High CPU is the symptom, not the cause — and replicas can make it worse if the real issue is a single bad plan. The migration in that deploy may have dropped an index, so a query that was an index seek is now a sequential scan burning CPU on every row. A replica just runs the same seq-scan on more machines. The actual evidence chain is: metric (p99 + CPU) points you, the slow-query log names the statement, and EXPLAIN shows "Seq Scan on orders" where you expected "Index Scan". CPU told you WHERE to look; only the query plan tells you WHY — and the fix is to restore the index, not the hardware.

observability-incidents.title: Observability is a three-layer evidence trail: metric points, log/trace explains, query plan confirms
observability-incidents.text: A database incident is diagnosed, not guessed. The invariant: every claim traces to evidence across three layers — a metric anchored to an SLO, a log or trace that names the failing work, and a query plan that confirms why the engine did it. Missing a layer means you are guessing.

observability-incidents.title: Tracing the incident from metric to query plan
observability-incidents.subtitle: The exact commands the on-call ran — each one narrows the search from "slow" to a dropped index.
observability-incidents.code:
-- 1. METRIC: which statements regressed since the deploy? (pg_stat_statements)
SELECT query, calls, mean_exec_time, rows
FROM pg_stat_statements
ORDER BY mean_exec_time DESC
LIMIT 5;
--   top row: SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = $1  mean=842ms (was 3ms)

-- 2. LOG/TRACE: confirm it on the live slow-query log + a trace span
--   log_min_duration_statement = 200ms  ->  orders read tagged on the checkout span

-- 3. QUERY PLAN: ask the engine WHY it is slow
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 4815162342;
--   Seq Scan on orders  (cost=0..98214 rows=1 width=240)
--     Filter: (customer_id = 4815162342)   Rows Removed by Filter: 8402911
--   Planning Time: 0.1ms   Execution Time: 841.7ms

-- 4. ROOT CAUSE: the index the planner wanted is gone
SELECT indexname FROM pg_indexes
WHERE tablename = 'orders' AND indexname = 'idx_orders_customer';
--   (0 rows)  -- last night's migration dropped it

steps.label: Metric layer — find the regressed statement
steps.note: pg_stat_statements ranks by mean_exec_time. The orders read jumped from 3ms to 842ms — that is your SLO breach, attributed to one query, not 'the DB is slow'.

steps.label: Log/trace layer — confirm it is real and live
steps.note: log_min_duration_statement surfaces it in the live log; the trace span ties it to the checkout request. Now you know it is THIS statement on THIS path, not a coincidence.

steps.label: Query-plan layer — ask the engine WHY
steps.note: EXPLAIN ANALYZE is the layer monitoring cannot give you. 'Seq Scan' with 8.4M rows removed by filter is the smoking gun: the planner has no index to seek, so it reads the whole table.

steps.label: Root cause — name the change that did it
steps.note: The index idx_orders_customer is gone. Cross-reference the migration: last night's deploy dropped it. Now you have metric → log → plan → cause, a chain a reviewer can replay.

observability-incidents.caption: Each step removes ambiguity the previous one left: the metric says which query, the log says it is live, the plan says why, and pg_indexes names the migration to roll back. That trail is the artifact.

observability-incidents.text: Standards grounding: SWEBOK V4 and ACM/IEEE CS2023 both treat operability and evidence-based diagnosis as core software-engineering competencies, and ABET Computing Outcomes require the ability to analyze a problem and identify solutions using evidence. The senior tell in a database incident is the same in all three: a claim about the cause that traces to a query plan, not to a guess about hardware. "Add a replica" without an EXPLAIN is a campaign; "Seq Scan on orders, index dropped by migration 0142" is a diagnosis a reviewer will sign.

observability-incidents.question: Reviewer challenge: an engineer says "checkout was slow, so I added two read replicas and it recovered." What is the strongest evidence that this was a real diagnosis and not a lucky patch?
options: A screenshot showing database CPU dropped after the replicas came online.

A signal trail: pg_stat_statements naming the regressed query, an EXPLAIN showing a Seq Scan from a dropped index, and the migration diff that dropped it — with the rollback that restored the index seek.
A note that latency returned to normal within fifteen minutes of the change.
A statement that the team agreed replicas were the standard fix for high CPU.
observability-incidents.explanation: Only option 2 is observability: a metric attributes the regression to one statement, a query plan confirms WHY (Seq Scan, no index), and the migration diff names the change to reverse. CPU dropping (1) and latency recovering (3) are correlations — replicas can mask a Seq Scan without fixing it, and the index is still gone for the next deploy. Team convention (4) is not evidence at all. The reviewer trusts the trail, not the recovery.

Plan: EXPLAIN shows Seq Scan, 8.4M rows filtered
Cause: migration 0142 dropped idx_orders_customer

observability-incidents.caption: Stale-symptom resolution ≠ root-cause resolution. The right column traces every claim to a metric, a plan, and a named migration — so the same regression cannot silently return, and the capstone can reuse the packet verbatim.

observability-incidents.symptom: After a migration, writes to orders intermittently hang for seconds and some checkout transactions time out — but EXPLAIN on the SELECT looks fine and CPU is normal. The metric layer alone says nothing useful.
observability-incidents.task: The symptom is lock contention, not a slow plan — so the right signal is the LOCK layer, not pg_stat_statements. Name the observability signal that exposes it and the safer migration shape.
observability-incidents.fix: Inspect pg_locks / pg_stat_activity (wait_event_type = 'Lock'): the long transaction holds an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock on orders for the whole rewrite, blocking every concurrent write until COMMIT. That is the signal a CPU/latency dashboard hides. The fix is to stop holding one giant lock: add the column with a cheap default, backfill risk_score in batched transactions outside the migration, and build the index with CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY so it does not lock writes. Same end state, no peak-hour ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock — and the rollback trigger watches lock-wait time, not just latency.

observability-incidents.intro: Prove your incident packet is observable — no vibes:
items: Every claim about the cause traces to a specific signal: name the metric (which query/SLO), the log or trace line, and the query plan. If any layer is missing, you are still guessing.
Run EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) on the suspect statement and confirm the plan matches your story — a Seq Scan, a missing index, or a lock wait, not just 'it's slow'.
Name the exact change that caused it (the migration, the dropped constraint, the new query path) — a cause you cannot name is a cause you cannot prevent.
Your rollback trigger is a concrete threshold a machine could evaluate (p99 > Xs for N min, lock-wait > Ys), not 'roll back if it feels bad'.
Identify the one instrumentation gap that would have caught this earlier (a plan-regression alert, a lock-wait alert, a slow-query threshold) and add it to the packet.

prompts: Walk the three layers using your own incident: which metric pointed you, which log or trace explained it, and what the query plan confirmed about WHY the engine was slow.
Explain to a junior why high CPU (or high latency) is a symptom, not a diagnosis — and what the query-plan layer gives you that no dashboard can.
State your rollback trigger out loud and defend the threshold: why that number, and what false-positive or false-negative it accepts.

observability-incidents.text: The three-layer trail is domain-independent: metric points, the explaining layer narrates, the ground-truth layer confirms. An SRE reads RED metrics → distributed traces → flame graphs; a doctor reads vitals → symptoms → the scan that confirms; a trader reads P&L → the trade log → the fill that explains the slip. What stays invariant is the chain from symptom to engine-level proof and a reversal trigger; what changes is the ground-truth tool — EXPLAIN here, a flame graph there. Carry schema_migration_decision_and_rollback_packet.md into the database capstone: it reuses this exact packet — the SLO-anchored symptom, the EXPLAIN proof, the named migration, and the rollback trigger — as its incident-readiness evidence. The portfolio claim is not 'I understand observability' but 'here is an incident I diagnosed across metric, log, and query plan, named the migration that caused it, and shipped a rollback trigger so it cannot silently return — read the packet.'

integration-mini-project.text: Friday, 5 p.m.: a product manager needs orders filterable by status, the migration that adds the index has been running for nine minutes holding a lock on the live orders table, and nobody wrote a way back. This lesson is the packet that turns that scene into a controlled, reversible change.

Everything Course 04 taught — schema, constraints, indexes, migrations, transactions, query plans, privacy, backups, data quality — was a single skill rehearsed alone. Production never sends them one at a time; this lesson welds them into one artifact that preserves truth under change, load, and bad input.

integration-mini-project.prompt: Your migration adds a NOT NULL status column to a 40M-row orders table and an index to make it queryable. What is the most likely thing to break in production — and what would prove it before you ship? Answer before reading on.
integration-mini-project.reveal: The NOT NULL is the trap, not the index. Adding a NOT NULL column with no default rewrites or rejects every existing row, and on Postgres an unbatched CREATE INDEX (not CONCURRENTLY) takes an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock that freezes reads and writes for the whole build. The proof is a dry-run on a production-sized copy that surfaces the lock wait and the constraint violation BEFORE the real run — exactly the autopsy the packet forces you to write down.

integration-mini-project.title: Writing the packet's proof, one statement at a time
integration-mini-project.subtitle: An end-to-end slice: forward migration in a transaction, the constraint, the indexed query path, and the rollback that makes it reversible.

steps.label: Add nullable, inside a transaction
steps.note: Migrations · transactions. Adding the column nullable first avoids the full-table rewrite a NOT-NULL-with-no-default would trigger. BEGIN makes the whole change atomic — it all lands or none of it does.

steps.label: Backfill before you constrain
steps.note: Data quality. You cannot demand NOT NULL while old rows are null. Backfill every existing row to a real value first — the order matters.

steps.label: The constraint that protects truth
steps.note: Constraints. SET NOT NULL is the invariant: from now on no order can exist without a status. This is the line a reviewer checks first.

steps.label: The new query path, no lock
steps.note: Indexes. CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY builds without the ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock that freezes a live table — the difference between a 9-minute outage and zero downtime.

steps.label: Prove the plan changed
steps.note: Query plans. EXPLAIN ANALYZE before and after is the evidence: Seq Scan over 40M rows at 1180 ms becomes an Index Scan at 6 ms. Without this, 'I added an index' is a claim, not a proof.

steps.label: The rollback — the reverse path
steps.note: The packet is only reversible if you wrote and ran the way back. DROP INDEX then DROP COLUMN returns the schema to its exact prior state — a two-way door, not a blind leap.

integration-mini-project.caption: A reviewer should run the forward block, see the plan flip Seq Scan → Index Scan, then run the rollback block and land back on the original schema — both directions, from your packet alone.

integration-mini-project.text: Standards grounding (SWEBOK V4 Software Configuration Management and Maintenance): the senior tell on a migration is not that it works — it's that the rollback was tested before the forward run shipped. (There is no SWEBOK 'data management' KA; controlled/reversible change belongs to Configuration Management.) Reviewers trust the engineer who can answer 'what happens when this is wrong at 2 a.m.?' with a script, not a shrug. Reversibility is the whole game; a one-way migration with no proven back path is an outage waiting for a trigger.

integration-mini-project.question: Reviewer challenge: you claim your migration packet is production-ready. Which single piece of evidence proves it is reversible and measured — not just a happy-path run?
options: The migration ran without an error on your local machine.

A backfill-then-SET-NOT-NULL forward block, an EXPLAIN ANALYZE before/after showing Seq Scan → Index Scan, AND a rollback script you executed on a production-sized copy to return the schema to its prior state.
The new column has a descriptive name and a comment.
You took a database backup before starting, so you could restore the whole database if needed.
integration-mini-project.explanation: Only option 2 proves both axes the packet exists to defend: measured (EXPLAIN before/after is evidence the index changed the plan, not a guess) and reversible (an executed rollback returns the schema to its exact prior state — a two-way door). A clean local run (1) tests nothing about production load or constraints; a name (3) is cosmetics; a full-database backup (4) is a blunt last resort, not a surgical, tested rollback — restoring 40M rows to undo one column is the failure this packet replaces.

integration-mini-project.intro: Prove the packet holds — replayable by a stranger, no vibes:
items: DDL diff present: a reader can see exactly which columns, constraints, and indexes changed — the before and after schema.
Migration dry-run ran on a production-sized copy and surfaced (not hid) the realistic failure — the lock wait or the NOT-NULL violation.
The constraint is named and tested: insert a row that violates it and confirm the database rejects it. If nothing rejects, the constraint isn't protecting truth.
EXPLAIN ANALYZE is captured before AND after; the new query path uses the index (Index Scan, not Seq Scan), with the actual-time delta recorded.
The rollback script was executed on a copy and returned the schema to its exact prior state — reversibility proven, not asserted.
Privacy boundary stated: any PII column is masked or explicitly declared out of scope, with a defensible reason.

Carry schema_migration_decision_and_rollback_packet.md straight into the database capstone; the capstone reuses this exact artifact and proof. You don't just describe a safe migration now. You can ship one and take it back.

database-capstone.text: Friday, 6 p.m.: a migration to add a unique index on (org_id, email) has been running for nine minutes, it just took an exclusive lock on the users table, every signup is timing out — and nobody wrote the rollback. The engineer who shipped a packet with a tested down-script is calm; the one who shipped a bare ALTER is on the phone with the VP.

This is the synthesis lesson of Databases and Data Modeling: every prior skill — schema design, constraints, indexes, transactions, migrations, query plans, privacy, backups, data quality — converges on one decision. The win is not understanding any one of them; it is assembling them into a packet that preserves truth under change, load, and bad input.

database-capstone.prompt: "The migration ran in staging with no errors, so it is safe to deploy." Before you ship it — what is the load-bearing thing that sentence quietly skips? Answer before reading on.
database-capstone.reveal: Two things, and both are about reversibility under real conditions. Staging has no production data volume, so a CREATE INDEX that returned instantly on 200 rows can hold an exclusive lock for minutes on 40M rows — the same DDL, a different blast radius. And "no errors forward" says nothing about backward: a migration without a tested down-script is an irreversible change wearing a reversible costume. The capstone bar is not "it ran" — it is "it ran, I can prove the new query path is faster, and I can put it back."

database-capstone.title: The migration + rollback, one statement at a time
database-capstone.subtitle: The forward DDL, the constraint promotion, and the tested down-script — the heart of schema_migration_decision_and_rollback_packet.md.

steps.label: Build the index CONCURRENTLY
steps.note: The naive path — ALTER TABLE ... ADD UNIQUE — takes an exclusive lock and blocks every write for the build. CONCURRENTLY trades a longer build for zero downtime on a 40M-row table. This is the index + transaction skill doing the real work.

steps.label: Promote index → constraint
steps.note: USING INDEX adopts the already-built index instead of rebuilding it, so the constraint add is near-instant. This is where the data model's invariant becomes an enforced constraint the database guarantees.

steps.label: Verify the invariant holds NOW
steps.note: Run BEFORE promoting in a dry run: if this returns any row, real duplicate data already violates the constraint and the ADD will fail. Data quality is checked, not assumed.

steps.label: The rollback — the part most people skip
steps.note: DROP CONSTRAINT then DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY returns the schema to its exact prior state. IF EXISTS makes the down-script idempotent so a half-applied migration can be retried. This is the line that turns a one-way door into a two-way door.

database-capstone.caption: A reviewer runs UP then DOWN against a scratch clone and gets back a byte-identical schema. That round-trip is the capstone proof.

database-capstone.title: A bare ALTER vs a migration packet
database-capstone.subtitle: Same change — add per-org unique email. One is a deploy; one is reviewable, reversible, and proven.

lines: ALTER TABLE users ADD UNIQUE (org_id, email)
Exclusive lock — blocks writes for the whole build
No duplicate-check: ADD just fails mid-deploy on real data
No rollback script — reversal is improvised at 6 p.m.
No EXPLAIN: cannot show the query path actually improved

Duplicate-check runs in the dry-run before promotion
Tested DOWN script restores byte-identical prior schema

lower(email) enforces the invariant case-insensitively

database-capstone.caption: The difference is not knowledge of ALTER — both know it. It is whether the invariant, the reversal, and the proof are on the page.

database-capstone.text: Standards grounding (interface/contract discipline; SWEBOK V4 Software Configuration Management treats changes as controlled contract-affecting events): a schema change is a contract change. (SWEBOK V4 has no 'data management' KA and does not state this.) The professional move the whole course builds toward is making that contract change reversible and observable — the rollback script proves reversibility, the EXPLAIN diff proves the new path, and the constraint proves the invariant survived. A change you cannot put back is technical debt you took on without a vote.

database-capstone.question: Reviewer challenge: which single piece of evidence best proves this migration packet is capstone-ready, not just understood?
options: The forward DDL ran without errors in staging.
A round-trip transcript: UP then DOWN against a scratch clone leaves a byte-identical schema, plus an EXPLAIN showing the new query path is an index scan.
A paragraph explaining why unique constraints matter.
The migration is short and reads cleanly.
database-capstone.explanation: Capstone readiness is reversibility + proof, not forward success. Option 2 demonstrates the rollback actually restores the prior state (two-way door) AND that the new index changed the query plan (the goal was met). Forward-only success (1), prose (3), and brevity (4) all leave the dangerous question — can you put it back, and did it work — unanswered.

database-capstone.intro: Prove the packet — no caps for vibes:
items: DDL diff present: the exact UP statements and the exact DOWN statements, both in the packet.
Migration dry-run transcript against a scratch clone shows UP applying cleanly, including the duplicate-check returning zero rows.
Rollback proven: DOWN runs and a schema diff against the pre-migration snapshot shows no difference.
Query-plan comparison: EXPLAIN (or EXPLAIN ANALYZE) before and after, showing the targeted query moved from a sequential scan to an index scan.
Constraint test: an INSERT of a known-duplicate (org_id, email) is rejected by the new constraint — the invariant is enforced, not just declared.
Reversal condition written: the concrete signal (e.g., lock held > 2 min, or backfill misses) that triggers running the DOWN script.

prompts: Roll-call the course: name the prior skills this packet reuses — schema/constraints, indexes, transactions, migrations, query plans, data quality, backups — and say what each one contributes to THIS change.
Explain why CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY plus USING INDEX is the safe path on a 40M-row table, using the lock behavior as the reason.

Your rollback ran clean. Explain, in your own words, why a tested DOWN script is what separates a reversible two-way door from an irreversible one — and when you would reach past it to a backup/PITR instead.

database-capstone.text: The same packet shape moves to any schema change under different pressure. Splitting a column into a new table is the same five sections with a backfill and a dual-write window; adding a NOT NULL is the same with a staged DEFAULT then a validated constraint; a privacy change (drop a PII column) is the same but the rollback must respect that the data should NOT come back, so the reversal door is a backup restore, not a re-add. What stays invariant: name the constraint, prove the new path, and never ship a forward without a tested backward. What changes is the reversal door and the proof — chosen by scale, risk, latency, and privacy. The packet you built is your portfolio evidence: not "I understand database migrations" but "here is a schema change I framed, made reversible, proved with a query plan, and rolled back clean — read it." That is the whole course, in your hands.
